He went on a club appearance tour, returning to Ibiza by private jet and earning a rumoured £60,000 a day. He cashed in with numerous freebies, including a yacht trip valued at over £10,000. And he reportedly commands £2,000 a post plugging goods and services on Instagram.

News.title: Mums and babies risk lives on mega-dinghies in desperate bid to get to UK
News.content:
This is the human face of the Channel boats crisis, desperate people on the final leg of a journey that could kill them.

Our exclusive images show young children, including some in pushchairs, being bussed to board mega-dinghies to get to Britain. Our investigators tracked a group of around 50 migrants, including small children and women earlier this week as they travelled around 40 miles south-west from France’s largest migrant camp at Loon-Plage, near Dunkirk, to Ecault Forest, close to Boulogne.

The group had paid around £1,200 each to make the final leg of their journey to the UK. They also paid extra for lifejackets, sold at stalls in the Loon-Plage camp for up to €50 (£42) – almost double the price in nearby shops.

View 8 Images Katie Sweetingham, head of operations at Care4Calais (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Express)

‌



English Channel horror as 157 migrants capsize on flaming boat with France and UK launching rescue mission READ MORE :

Three migrants die crossing the Channel after busiest day this year READ MORE :

Katie Sweetingham, Head of Operations at charity Care4Calais, says she has seen increasing numbers of women and children, including babies, at the camp since the UK government indefinitely paused family reunion applications in September last year. She said: “Lots of women and children would use that scheme to be reunited with their loved ones in the UK and now that option is not available. So they have to get into a boat and make that dangerous crossing.”

The journey we saw the migrants make on Thursday seemed complicated. After being taken from the camp to a bus stop in Loon-Plage, the group boarded a bus to Gravelines. Following a lengthy wait, they then took a second bus from Gravelines to Calais, before boarding a train to Boulogne, where they got on another bus to the edge of the forest.

View 8 Images Migrants in Boulogne where they were preparing to take their third bus journey of the day (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Express)

On getting off the final bus, they made their way along hiking paths to a makeshift dwelling inside the protected natural site, which includes various camping spots for caravans. They appeared to be being guided by a tall man, believed to be Kurdish, who had a distinctive tattoo on his right hand.

‌



French police, including armed gendarmes, followed the migrants throughout the four-hour journey, including walking with them into the forest. But they made no attempt to stop them.

Good weather has led to perfect sailing conditions so far this summer, causing a spike in crossing attempts by gangs. Four migrants, including three women, have died in separate boat tragedies in the Channel in recent days. And with the favourable conditions now expected to continue until at least September, there are fears of more tragedies. Investigators say traffickers are increasingly exploiting the Opal Coast, south of Boulogne, to launch dangerously overloaded rubber boats following a crackdown further north in Calais and Dunkirk.

View 8 Images Stalls, linked to the smuggling gangs, at Loon-Plage migrant camp are selling life jackets for 50 Euros (Image: Humphrey Nemar/ daily Mirror)

They use new mega-dinghies bought from manufacturers in China. Despite being completely unfit for open seas, the boats are being used to transport more than 150 migrants at a time, netting the gangs up to £200,000 for a single trip. Ordering a mega-dinghy previously took months and involved a 5,500-mile journey by road, via countries including Kazakhstan and Turkey, costing traffickers at least £10,000.

‌



However, we can reveal at least one factory is now offering direct delivery by plane to France, in packages measuring just 2m x 1m x 1m. The vessels are advertised online as Huge Large Super Inflatable Pontoon Rescue Boats, and cost just £1,200. But they are billed as being designed for 40 people, not 150. The maximum delivery time is just two weeks.

View 8 Images Police patrol the beach at Équihen Plage on the lookout for migrants trying to board mega dinghies (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

Katie said: “We’ve heard about the bigger dinghies from the people we support. It’s a recent change. It just goes to show that all of the border security measures, largely funded by the UK, don’t do their stated aim of stopping the crossings. All they do is make people that are organising the crossings change their business model, which is now the larger boats, making it much more dangerous for the people that are attempting crossings.”

Katie says she and her team regularly meet children as young as 13 trying to cross to Britain without adult supervision. She said: “It’s usually going to be those younger people that are targeted for driving the boat and then on entry to the UK they’re much more likely to be criminalised and not believed for their age.”

‌



View 8 Images A group of Iraqi Kurdish migrants walk down the main road into Equihen Plage, a popular migrant beach for onward small boat transport to Britain (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

A week last Thursday, a boat overturned in the water near Ecault Forest, causing the death of a man and leading to the near-drowning of a baby. The same day, three women in their 20s, 30s and 40s, drowned after an inflatable dinghy with more than 100 people on board capsized near Loon-Plage.

Katie said: “More people are dying trying to make the journey. A lot of them speak to us and say they’ve been on a boat and they’ve seen their friends die in front of them, but then they will say ‘what else can I do?’ There’s no other way for that person to be able to reach safety in the UK to be able to gain asylum other than to repeat that journey again and try again.”

8 View 8 Images Migrants walking down the main road into Equihen Plage on Saturday (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com) 8 View 8 Images Migrants were also seen wandering the many trails inside Écault Forest while waiting for an opportunity to board boats to Britain (Image: Charlie Varley/varleypix.com)

‌



Figures have just revealed the average number of migrants crammed per boat has more than doubled over five years. Analysis found 66 migrants on average have been packed on to each of the 219 vessels to cross the Channel successfully this year. They carried 14,561 passengers in total. An average of 27 per boat was recorded for the whole of 2021, when 1,064 vessels carrying 28,526 migrants made it to the Kent coast.

A source said: “These so-called mega-dinghies are hugely profitable and the smugglers are getting hold of them very easily. Their emergence means a huge number of people can be moved at one time, but always in extremely and increasingly dangerous circumstances. Frankly, it is a nightmare development for the authorities.”

An Egyptian man yesterday began a one-year prison sentence in France after being convicted of trying to smuggle a record 173 migrants into Britain on a 40ft mega-dinghy that burst into flames in the Channel. An Iraqi-born people-smuggler, named by police as Rasoul Halo, was on Tuesday also imprisoned for a year, for smuggling an inflatable boat on to a beach. Halo, who was found with three passports including a British one, claimed he was just helping a friend with a delivery.

News.title: Days out at UK seaside considered outdated as young people moan about seagulls, toilets and phone woes
News.content:
Days out at UK seaside considered outdated as young people moan about seagulls, toilets and phone woes

The poll, commissioned by eco-tech brand Hive, found eight in ten of people aged between 14 and 29 are no longer fond of visits to Britain's seaside resorts

View 3 Images Seagulls pinching chips is one of the major moans (Image: Getty Images)

The tide is turning on traditional bucket and spade beach holidays, according to research.

‌



A poll found 80% of those aged 14 to 29 reckon a day at the British seaside was old fashioned. And the Love Island generation weren’t slow to explain why a trip to the sea gives them the ick.

‌



The major moan for 70% of the 2,000 young people was their phone running out of juice. But other sources of stress include filthy toilets, problems finding a car parking space and seagulls swooping in to nick their chips. Physical conditions of the beach can also be annoying.

‌



View 3 Images Many are miffed by sand in shoes (Image: Getty Images/Connect Images)

Moment seaside cafe owner saves drowning children by throwing life rings READ MORE :

UK Heatwave: Yellow heat alerts issued as temperatures set to soar to 36C READ MORE :

People shared complaints it is too far from the car, the sea’s too cold, they get sand on their feet, or it is too pebbly. Phones seem to matter to Gen Z more than enjoying a day out.

‌



Many say poor signal does their head in or panic their tech will get trashed. More than one in 10 moan they can’t see their screen in the sun, and nearly as many sulk as there’s nowhere to charge their phone.

While 70% say a dying battery ruins the day, just 37% of Baby Boomers, aged 62 to 80, who managed to survive childhood without a portable power bank, agree. Three in 10 Gen Z and over a quarter of Millennials, aged 30 to 45, have left the beach early because their phone was running low.

View 3 Images Low phone battery was also a big concern cited by respondents to the poll (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Article continues below

Susan Wells, of eco-tech brand Hive, which commissioned the poll, said: “When the weather heats up, Britain heads to the coast, but beaches rarely offer power. Dead phones and no charging points have become a familiar frustration, especially when people rely on their devices for digital tickets, maps, messaging and mobile payments.”

Brits enjoy at least four beach days every summer with 90% saying that some of their best summer memories are from time spent there, proving a little sand in your shoes is still a price many are willing to pay.

When it comes to the most nostalgic seaside holiday memories from childhood, eating fish and chips wrapped in newspaper at the beach is rated by 55%, followed by more than half who valued time with the whole family. Other highlights include penny arcades, collecting seashells and eating sticks of rock.

News.title: Victims urged to come forward as police accused of 'litany of failures' over murderer and rapist
News.content:
Police have urged more victims of Simon Levy to come forward, as London's victims' commissioner said a "litany of failures" had allowed him to kill two women and rape a third.

Andrea Simon called for a review on the "failure to monitor him appropriately" when the 40-year-old was known to police as a sexual predator.

British Transport Police said women who recognised Levy as their attacker should report it, while the Met Police said it had investigated whether he had more victims, including further murders.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable is under investigation for gross misconduct, and a detective sergeant is facing a misconduct investigation.

On Friday, Levy was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London while he was being monitored by the Met Police for being a convicted sex offender. He had previously committed a string of sex attacks.

The BBC reported how a series of grave failings by police, prosecutors and the courts left Levy free to murder, rape and sexually assault women.

Levy is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Chasing a ghost: How BBC tracked a fugitive spy chief after months-long hunt
News.content:
For months we drew a blank in our hunt for Luka.

And then we had our first breakthrough.

One of those listed in the book, who we tried calling again, finally answered the phone.

He had been the guard for Luka's apartment block, he told us, and eventually agreed to give us the number for someone he said had been Luka's personal bodyguard - a man we are calling Mahmoud.

It took weeks to secure an interview with Mahmoud. Meetings would be scheduled but he would not show up, or he would request a meeting in a private space such as a car or apartment, which our reporter judged too much of a risk.

They eventually met at a hotel one night, just before midnight. Broad-shouldered and physically imposing, Mahmoud seemed to be considering every answer carefully before he spoke.

He told us he was angry with Luka for leaving him behind when the regime fell. As word had spread in December 2024 that Assad's rule was on the brink of collapse - with rebels advancing on the capital - Luka had said he would stay and defend Damascus, Mahmoud told us. But by the early hours of the next morning, Luka had disappeared, taking a large sum of money with him from the office safe, Mahmoud said.

Mahmoud refused to share any contact details for Luka or his family, but did give us a number for Luka's driver, who he believed had driven the former spy chief out of the capital that night.

This man proved even harder to reach.

When he answered the phone, his voice was nervous and unsteady. He repeatedly insisted he was just a driver, and knew nothing of Luka's activities. Multiple meetings with us were never kept, and eventually he stopped replying.

We turned our attention to Luka's possible escape routes, including neighbouring Lebanon - where the Iran-backed group Hezbollah had close links with the Assad regime.

One senior source in the Lebanese government told us he understood Luka had passed through Lebanon on a "good Russian passport but with a different name", before flying out to Russia.

We managed to find a man, now based in Lebanon, whose name was listed in Luka's contacts book, but under a number that no longer worked. He is one of many wanted by the new Syrian government, because of his close association with the Assad regime.

This man, who we cannot identify, said he had a number for Luka.

We saw it, and realised it had a Russian country code.

Russia was a key backer of the Assad regime, and in the days after his fall, Assad released a statement confirming that he had fled there. Many of his inner circle were believed to have followed him.

Back in Luka's apartment in Damascus, we had found clues that Luka also had strong links to Moscow - awards from Russia's foreign spy service, and even a New Year's card addressed to him from a senior Russian official.

Now, the Russian telephone number for him suggested we finally had proof that he was - as we had predicted - in Russia.

News.title: Sturgeon hasn't spoken to Murrell since he was jailed for embezzling SNP funds
News.content:
Sturgeon also told Dale that she only discovered Murrell was due to plead guilty a week before his first public court appearance.

It later emerged he had been negotiating his plea for months, a fact which she said "hit me like a tonne of bricks".

Sturgeon said: "He was still lying to me right up until the day he pled guilty."

The former first minister added: "He was very isolated over that period, he very rarely left the house, he wasn't communicative, I was a bit worried about his well-being and his mental health.

"And then, now I think: 'What a mug, why were you worried about him?' He didn't worry about me. He didn't worry at all about what he was doing.

"What he has subjected me to is beyond anything I could ever have comprehended.

"I don't understand why he did it, he had no need to do it, I don't think I will ever understand his motivations.

"But whatever that motivation was, he could not have stopped and ever thought about me.

"But I was, until recently, still worrying about him."

Sturgeon - who had stepped down as first minister in March 2023 - was arrested In June 2023 but was later told that she was no longer under investigation.

The former first minister announced her separation from Murrell last year.

News.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
News.content:
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

News.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
News.content:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

News.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back and 'a bit more real'
News.content:
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention â "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right â digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18â30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids â where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image â are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

News.title: How a former GB Olympian curbed his porn problem - and the signs and steps to recovery
News.content:
Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn.

"Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.

By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.

Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset.

"You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said.

So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?

Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right.

"We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.

But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" â like someone might experience with drugs, for example â and how best to deal with it.

Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.

This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.

Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.

This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.

The NHS does say, external it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Strictly dancers Ola and James Jordan separate after 23 years of marriage
News.content:
Former Strictly Come Dancing stars James and Ola Jordan have confirmed they have separated after more than 20 years of marriage.

The former professional dancers were regulars on the show for several series after first featuring in 2006.

The couple in a statement said they were "taking some time apart as we work through very difficult personal challenges".

"This has been an incredibly painful and emotional journey for us both and it certainly wasn't an easy decision," they said in a joint post shared on their Instagram accounts.

The couple said James had moved out the family home some time ago and they "don't know exactly what the future holds".

"Right now, more than anything we ask for kindness, empathy and a little privacy as we work through this as a family."

The couple's manager Vickie White had prevously said in a statement: "It is with great sadness that I can confirm that James and Ola began a trial separation some time ago

"Their shared priority remains co-parenting their daughter, Ella, and they are committed to putting her wellbeing first.

"They would greatly appreciate your understanding as they navigate this difficult time."

Ola Jordan won the Open Polish Championship in 1999 when she was 17 years old and became James' dance partner shortly afterwards in March 2000.

She moved to England a month later and the pair got married in October 2003.

James appeared on Strictly from 2006 to 2013 while Ola appeared on the show until 2015.

Ola's celebrity partners included wildlife presenter Steve Backshall and Welsh sprinter Iwan Thomas, while James danced with former international gymnast and broadcaster Gabby Logan, as well as The One Show presenter Alex Jones.

News.title: Charity watchdog investigates aid charity over alleged Hamas links
News.content:
A UK-based aid charity is being investigated by counter-terror police and the charity watchdog over alleged links to Hamas.

The Charity Commission launched an inquiry into Muslim faith-based charity Al-Khair Foundation on Friday.

Counter Terror Policing London (CTP) also confirmed investigations into the charity, with two search warrants on addresses in Croydon, South London.

The foundation said it is "co-operating fully" with the inquiry and had filed a serious incident report with the watchdog before it was launched.

A spokesperson for the foundation said: "Everywhere we work we are firmly committed to ensuring that the funds entrusted to us by our generous donors are used for their intended purpose: meeting the humanitarian needs of poor and marginalised people in the communities we serve.

"Al-Khair Foundation is deeply committed to supporting those in need in Gaza. Our significant support over many years has included providing food parcels, hot meals, clean water, medical aid, shelter materials, winter assistance and orphan and family support."

The Al-Khair Foundation provides emergency relief and developmental support in "some of the world's most impoverished areas", according to its website.

Hamas is designated as a terrorist organisation by the UK and US governments.

It comes after last week Mohammad Yousef Hasna, 45, from Istanbul, Turkey, was arrested in the UK over US accusations of conspiring to funnel money and supplies to Hamas through a "sham charity".

The US Department of Justice did not name the "sham charity" in their press release.

The Al-Khair foundation maintains that Hasna is not an employee but works with one of its global partners to enable the delivery of aid around the world.

Hasna is being held following his arrest by the UK's National Crime Agency (NCA) and pending extradition proceedings before he can be taken to New York to face the US charges.

The US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York alleged Hasna used his senior role at a "purported global humanitarian organisation to coordinate directly with Hamas's senior leadership regarding the delivery of funds and supplies to Gaza, and the distribution of those funds and supplies at Hamas leadership's instructions".

Hasna is charged with conspiring to provide material support to Hamas, conspiring to finance terrorism and financing terrorism.

Each charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, the US Department of Justice said.

US Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said: "The money that flows from sham charities like the one described in the complaint fuels Hamas's terrorist activities, including the atrocities the group committed on October 7".

The Charity Commission said the Al-Khair Foundation recorded an income of more than Â£74m in the financial year ending 31 July 2025. The commission added it was made aware of the allegations against Hasna and "immediately started examining the serious concerns raised".

"The commission has now escalated its engagement to a statutory inquiry," the commission added.

Al-Khair is also subject to a legal order restricting some financial transactions being made without the consent of the Charity Commission.

News.title: Hundreds flying out of Birmingham Airport left without luggage
News.content:
She described seeing a "build up" of luggage at the airport, after problems with the luggage belt, but had been assured by staff that it would be loaded on to the plane.

But on arrival at Dalaman they were told by the pilot that no bags had been loaded.

"We have heard nothing about compensation, no communication when our luggage is expected, we've heard nothing about who is liable for it. Is it the airport? Is it TUI? Is it our travel insurance? Who are we meant to go to? We've had nothing from anybody", Chapman said.

"It's just radio silence from the airport, apart from literally telling people 'we've got an issue'".

The first day of their holiday was spent travelling to a shopping centre to buy essentials for "for the next few days" but she added "we have no idea how long this is going to last".

"There are families all over the world at the moment with nothing and no idea of what's going on," she said.

"It's really important that Birmingham Airport are held accountable, and sort this out."

News.title: Man guilty of fatal shooting of teen outside club
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of fatally shooting an 18-year-old outside a Wembley nightclub.

Tyrece Balcha was found with gunshot wounds outside the Crystal Club in Atlantic Crescent at about 05:30 GMT on 21 September 2025. He was taken to hospital, where he died four days later.

A jury at the Old Bailey found Ashley Wallace, 40, of Shenley Road, Southwark, guilty of murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

At the same trial, two men were found not guilty of murder. A woman was cleared of possession of a firearm, possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life, and perverting the course of justice. The jury did not reach a verdict on a fourth man.

CCTV footage showed that Balcha had been involved in an altercation inside the club before being followed outside and shot.

Wallace fled the scene in a vehicle and was arrested on 25 September after police traced the car to south-east London.

A revolver carrying Wallace's DNA was found inside the vehicle, and investigators established that the bullet recovered from the murder scene had been fired from the gun.

News.title: Siân Phillips to step back from acting aged 93 after memory issues
News.content:
One of Wales' most celebrated actresses, Dame SiÃ¢n Phillips, is stepping back from full-scale stage acting after experiencing memory issues during rehearsals.

The 93-year-old made the decision after struggling to remember her lines while preparing for a recent production, according to The Times.

However, Phillips said she would continue performing in smaller projects, including a production with Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Her career has spanned more than 80 years across stage, television and film.

Phillips told The Times she decided to stop taking on major stage productions after struggling to remember her lines during rehearsals for Atonement at Chichester Festival Theatre earlier this year.

According to the newspaper, she said she would continue performing in her show It's All Greek and is also due to appear in Samuel Beckett's Rockaby for Michael Sheen's Welsh National Theatre next year.

Born in Betws, near Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, in 1933, Phillips grew up speaking Welsh before learning English by listening to the radio.

She began performing as a child, appearing on Welsh-language radio from the age of 11, before studying at the University of Wales and later winning a scholarship to the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art.

She performed in radio productions such as The Archers and an adaptation of John le Carre's Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy, opposite Sir Alec Guinness.

Before her acting career took off, she worked for BBC Wales as a bilingual announcer and newsreader.

Phillips went on to become one of Britain's most acclaimed actresses, appearing in productions including Doctor Who, Calendar Girls, Dune, and I, Claudius.

She won a Bafta for her portrayal of Livia in the BBC's I, Claudius and received a Tony Award nomination for playing the title role in Marlene.

She was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 2000 for services to drama, and then a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE) in 2016.

News.title: The 'cheap Cotswolds' attracting new residents
News.content:
More people are leaving cities behind in search of cheaper homes, more space and easier access to the countryside, with the Forest of Dean emerging as an increasingly popular destination for buyers priced out of nearby Bristol.

The Gloucestershire district, which lies between the River Severn and the Welsh border, has long been known for its ancient woodlands, market towns and rural communities.

Estate agents say it is now drawing new residents from across the South West who want countryside living without the price tag associated with the nearby Cotswolds.

Local estate agent Glen Webb said many buyers see the area as a more affordable alternative to one of England's most sought-after rural locations: "The Forest is really such a brilliant asset to Gloucestershire. It's a cheap version of the Cotswolds and people sort of love it for that reason."

News.title: Bristol Airport disruption a 'shambles' as flights restart
News.content:
Widespread disruption continues at Bristol Airport after a runway defect saw all flights suspended.

Hundreds of passengers were stranded after the airport's runway was closed from 18:00 BST on Friday until 08:00 on Saturday. While the runway has since reopened, the airport's website says the majority of flights are delayed or cancelled.

A spokesperson for the airport apologised for any inconvenience caused and advised passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.

Dave Blackwell, travelling home from the Greek island of Rhodes, said it had been "a shambles" since his flight back to Bristol was diverted to Newcastle.

"We were in Rhodes Airport for three hours with no information. Now we have all been told our flight is going to Newcastle and then a five or six-hour bus ride - why Newcastle? How appalling," he said.

British Columbia has declared a state of emergency as a rapidly spreading wildfire devastates communities, forcing over 20,000 residents to evacuate their homes along Okanagan Lake in western Canada.

Premier David Eby announced the emergency Saturday, with over 100 wildfires currently raging across the province. Nearly half of these blazes are out of control, fueled by hot, windy conditions and a prolonged drought.

The entire community of Summerland, home to approximately 12,000 people, received overnight evacuation orders, alongside 8,000 individuals in and around nearby Peachland. Officials have yet to determine how many homes were destroyed.

Eby confirmed some residents became trapped and required rescue, while search-and-rescue teams continue to comb areas behind fire lines for any others who may have been caught.

Nearly half of these blazes are out of control, fueled by hot, windy conditions and a prolonged drought ( Gary Nylander/The Canadian Press via AP )

“I know many families are facing an unimaginable day today,” Eby said. “People have lost their homes. And many people have been displaced. Others are waiting for news about loved ones.”

Cliff Chapman, director of wildfire operations for the BC Wildfire Service, said firefighting helicopters were diverted to rescue people who could no longer escape by road. He said the outcome would have been significantly worse without cooperation among agencies responding to the fire.

The Bald Range wildfire was first reported on Friday evening but grew to about 50 square kilometers (19 square miles) within hours, overwhelming the smaller community of Faulder and covering the roughly 15 kilometers (9 miles) to Summerland at extraordinary speed.

Chapman described fire conditions across British Columbia as “explosive” and warned that other communities could face fires similar to the one that forced the evacuation of Summerland.

British Columbia Emergency Management Minister Kelly Greene said the state of emergency gives the province additional powers, including the ability to restrict travel and secure accommodations for evacuees that might otherwise be unavailable.

Erick Thompson, an emergency official with the Regional District of Okanagan-Similkameen, called it one of the “quickest-moving, fastest-growing” wildfires the region had experienced.

Thompson eventually had to abandon the emergency operations center and evacuate his own family.

“I had to leave the EOC to come and get my family to leave this area. We’re heading south,” he said in a video posted early Saturday from his vehicle as traffic backed up around him.

Videos posted on social media appeared to show multiple homes burning as residents fled along roads with flames on both sides.

Homeowner Kerry Gold and her husband, Mike Elsinga, fled around 12:30 a.m. after watching flames spread beyond nearby mountains.

“It’s scary. It’s moving fast,” Gold said.

The couple, who recently moved from the city of Vancouver, had packed bags, prepared a carrier for their cat and planned to help a disabled friend evacuate.

“You want to stay here and protect your home, but you also don’t want to get caught in it,” Elsinga said.

Canada has endured increasingly destructive wildfire seasons in recent years, forcing mass evacuations and repeatedly sending smoke across large parts of Canada and the United States.

He didn’t score many points in his brief stint in the pros — but an ex-NBA player running for Congress appears to be going to great lengths to make one.

Former NBA bust and current Republican Senate candidate Royce White has announced plans to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft, claiming he now identifies as transgender — for athletic purposes, anyway.

“I’m transgender. I’m a woman. I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball, professional basketball, so I’ll be declaring for the WNBA draft in 2027 as well,” White, 35, told Fox News Saturday.

White’s announcement comes one day after former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom, who is a man, said he also plans to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft. Freedom’s statement followed comments from WNBA player Sophie Cunningham about transgender athletes that renewed a heated debate on the league’s policies for transgender players. It also comes as President Donald Trump has made barring transgender women from from competing in women’s sports.

White, a 6’8” forward who played just three games in the NBA, all in 2014, continued Saturday, “I think I’d be unstoppable. But I’m a team-first guy. I’m a pass-first kind of player. I do the little things. I led my team in all five major stat categories at Iowa State University, so I do a little bit of everything. I’ll do whatever the coach needs me to do. I’ll do whatever the girls need me to do.”

open image in gallery Former NBA player and U.S. Senate candidate Royce White announced Saturday that he plans to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft amid controversy over the league’s transgender eligibility policies ( AP )

“I think it’s only fair,” he added.

Freedom said he reviewed the WNBA’s eligibility rules before announcing his plans to enter the league and believes he meets the requirements to play.

The WNBA’s 2026 collective bargaining agreement states in Article XIII that “only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA.” However, the 409-page agreement does not define what qualifies as a “woman” for eligibility purposes.

Following Freedom’s announcement, the Women’s National Basketball Players Association said in a statement: “We embrace justice equity, diversity, and inclusion. Those are the values that unite this Union and allow it to protect women’s sports while creating transformational change.”

“Hate, abuse, and demonization of any person or group of people, including transgender people, only fuel fear, division, and harm. We will continue to have hard conversations,” the group added in the Instagram post. “But we will not be used as political pawns.”

White said Saturday that the WNBA could end the controversy by clearly stating its policy on whether males are eligible to compete in women’s sports.

“I think the WNBA could come out and make a definitive statement about guys with a pair of balls playing in the Women’s Association,” he said, adding he will continue moving forward in his draft bid unless the league addresses the controversial issue.

In a memo obtained by the Associated Press, WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told teams that a discussion about the inclusion of trans athletes “will continue to receive significant attention.”

“I wanted to reach out to share how we are approaching these conversations at the league office and to thank those of you who have responded to questions from the media with thoughtfulness and professionalism,” she wrote Friday.

“We recognize that this is a complex and nuanced topic, and we will continue to have important conversations with all of you and the Players Association in the weeks and months ahead,” Engelbert continued. “We also plan to convene additional discussions and offer listening sessions for any team leaders who would like to participate. Your perspectives and feedback are invaluable, and I appreciate those who have already reached out to share their thoughts.”

open image in gallery Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was the first to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft on Friday ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery The WNBA’s transgender athlete debate intensified in July after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham criticized trans participation in women’s sports ( Getty )

White further claimed he could take legal action if he is not drafted or signed by a WNBA team.

“I have to file a discrimination lawsuit, right? I mean, that’s, that’s ridiculous,” he told Fox News. “We’re gonna have to have a huge legal battle about discrimination if I can’t play.”

White was selected 16th overall by the Houston Rockets in the 2012 NBA Draft out of Iowa State but never played for the team because of severe anxiety and a fear of flying.

Nowadays, he is running in Minnesota’s August 11 Republican primary for U.S. Senate. White previously ran as the Republican nominee against Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar in 2024 but lost the general election.

The debate over transgender athletes in the WNBA intensified last month after Cunningham, a guard for the Indiana Fever, criticized trans participation in women’s sports.

“I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” Cunningham told ESPN, later doubling down on her comments, claiming they were “common sense.”

The Independent has contacted the WNBA and WNBPA for comment.

Fifa has hit out at what it described as attempts to “undermine” its embattled president, Gianni Infantino.

Infantino has faced calls to resign from his role in the aftermath of a saga that saw him abandon a proposed plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other Fifa competitions.

That proposal brought the threat of a boycott from Uefa, European football’s governing body, with England’s Football Association (FA) among those to officially withdraw their support for the Fifa president.

Infantino is due to seek re-election in March of next year. He has received backing from South American body Conmebol and the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

open image in gallery Fifa president Gianni Infantino is under pressure ( AP )

Infantino succeeded Sepp Blatter as president of Fifa in February 2016 having previously served as Uefa’s general secretary for seven years.

Infantino has strongly denied a claim made by The Telegraph that Uefa paid off his alleged lover with a six-figure sum during his time working at European football’s governing body, and has now been given fresh backing by Fifa.

“Echoing the recent statements of Conmebol and Caf, as well as discussions with Fifa Member Associations and Confederations from around the world, Fifa will not support, facilitate or tolerate any process concerning the election of the Fifa President that is inconsistent with Fifa’s Statutes, democratic procedures and established governance framework,” a Fifa spokesperson said. “The Fifa President was democratically elected by Fifa’s Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate.

open image in gallery Fifa’s management board backed Infantino at a meeting in Morocco on Wednesday (Sam Corum/PA) ( PA Wire )

“It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its President. Those who do not have the support of FIFA’s Member Associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa’s established democratic processes.

“Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning Fifa and its President. Speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact, and repetition does not make an allegation true.

“The Fifa President has dedicated more than 30 years of his professional life to European and world football, contributing to significant change in the game and, in particular, to broadening access, resources and opportunity across world football. Change inevitably challenges established interests, but disagreement with that change cannot justify efforts to undermine the democratic mandate of Fifa’s President or the institution he was elected to lead.

“Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress. Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, Fifa will challenge it directly and vigorously.

“Fifa’s responsibility is to its 211 Member Associations and to football around the world. We will not be distracted or diverted from strengthening the organisation, delivering for our Member Associations and continuing the work of making football truly global. Through the FIfa President and the Fifa administration, our focus remains firmly on that mission, and we are more determined than ever to fulfil it.”

Uefa has said that its threat to boycott remains in place despite the abandonment of the sell-off plans.

Fifa’s management board backed Infantino at a meeting in Morocco on Wednesday.

Common painkillers including ibuprofen could increase the chance of getting sunburn, Britain’s health watchdog has warned as the country braces for its fifth blistering heatwave of the summer.

The public is urged to take extra precautions if taking the medicine in warmer weather, with temperatures set to soar to 36C next week.

The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) said on Friday that drugs like ibuprofen and naproxen could increase sensitivity to the sun, making burns more likely.

Other treatments that can increase sensitivity include antibiotics like doxycycline and tetracycline, acne treatments like isotretinoin and topical retinoids, and antifungal medicines such as voriconazole.

open image in gallery A person drinks from a bottle while sat on sun-scorched grass at Victoria Tower Gardens ( AFP/Getty )

Dr Alison Cave, chief safety officer at the MHRA, said: “Some commonly used medicines can affect the body’s ability to stay hydrated, regulate temperature, or protect itself from sun exposure.

“Simple precautions can make a significant difference. Staying hydrated, avoiding the strongest sun during the middle of the day, and using protective clothing and sunscreen can all help reduce risk.”

She noted diuretics, often prescribed for blood pressure or heart conditions, can increase fluid loss and make dehydration more likely.

Meanwhile, some antidepressants and antipsychotics can affect the body’s ability to regulate temperature, and medicines like beta blockers may reduce the body’s response to heat stress.

The body uses several mechanisms to regulate temperature: sweating, blood flow to the skin and fluid balance. But some commonly prescribed drugs interfere with these processes, making it harder to stay cool.

Older adults, people with chronic conditions – especially those with heart or lung disease – and those taking multiple prescription drugs are especially vulnerable to heat-related illnesses.

open image in gallery The public is urged to take extra precautions if taking the medicine in warmer weather ( PA )

Last month, doctors warned people on certain mental health medications to take extra precautions ahead of another heatwave.

Dr Nick Broughton, NHS England’s national director for mental health, learning disabilities and autism, said that people taking antipsychotic medication and antidepressants need to be extra cautious during hot weather because some of these medicines can make it harder to keep the body cool.

“Most importantly, they should not stop taking their medication suddenly and can speak to their GP, pharmacist or mental health team for advice if they need to,” he said.

New yellow health heat alerts came into force this week as the UK prepares to face its fifth heatwave of the summer.

The alerts run until 9pm on Tuesday across all of England, except the North East and North West.

They warn that the hot weather is likely to affect the wellbeing of the population, particularly those who are vulnerable or have health conditions.

Luxury car manufacturer Mercedes AMG is facing a class-action lawsuit from two drivers who allege the prominent AMG logo on their vehicle's driver's seat becomes so hot it causes burns and literally brands them.

Gabriel Lahijani and Karendeep "Karina" Bath are the plaintiffs in the suit, filed earlier this week in the U.S. District Court of California’s Western Division.

They claim the front seats of certain Mercedes AMG cars contain a design flaw where the raised metallic AMG logo is "reasonably expected to contact an occupant’s upper back, neck, or shoulder."

The plaintiffs are seeking compensation from Mercedes for medical expenses, as well as for any pain, suffering, and emotional distress they can prove at trial. They also demand that Mercedes cover the cost for other owners to have the problematic logo removed from their vehicles.

open image in gallery The plaintiffs demand that Mercedes cover the cost for other owners to have the problematic logo removed from their vehicles. ( Mercedes-AMG )

Mercedes-Benz couldn’t be reached immediately for comment.

Lahigani, a Los Angeles resident, had leased a new 2026 Mercedes-AMG E-Class vehicle from an authorized Mercedes-Benz dealership in Los Angeles, according to the suit. He reported receiving second-degree burns on his back on May 31, after entering his vehicle wearing a tank top. A board-certified dermatologist subsequently documented first- and second-degree burns, describing the injury as “AMG inscribed."

Roughly six weeks later, Bath, a Chatsworth, California resident, received similar burns allegedly from the logo design while wearing a sleeveless top. After parking her Mercedes-AMG vehicle in Los Angeles, Bath returned to the vehicle and entered the driver’s seat, the suit said. Her shoulder immediately touched the logo, causing a burning sensation. In the following days, a mark in the shape of the AMG logo “darkened and became visible on her skin, consistent with a thermal contact burn," the lawsuit said.

In December, Mercedes-Benz USA and parent company Daimer AG agreed to pay $149.6 million to settle allegations that the automaker secretly installed devices in hundreds of thousands of vehicles to pass emission tests, according to an announcement by a coalition of attorneys general.

According to the coalition, between 2008 and 2016 the German automaker equipped more than 211,000 diesel passenger cars and vans with software devices that optimized emission controls during tests but reduced the controls during normal operations.

Jeepers creepers!

A New Jersey couple got a terrifying backyard surprise when they discovered an 8-foot Burmese python slithered beneath their shed — and its latest meal made the massive snake even harder to remove.

Leslie Daley was watering flowers at the family’s Freehold home when she spotted the enormous snake moving through the backyard, her husband, Ed, told ABC 7.

The Daleys then spotted a hole in the corner of the shed, where they believe the python crawled inside. They called the Monmouth County SPCA, setting off an unusual rescue operation.

“When the homeowner sent us a video of what we were actually dealing with, and when we all saw it, our jaws kind of dropped a little because that is a Burmese python, which definitely does not belong out in the wild in New Jersey,” Scott Crawford, an Animal Control Manager with the Monmouth County SPCA, told the news outlet.

open image in gallery A New Jersey couple found an 8-foot, 40-pound Burmese python under their shed, and its full belly made the massive snake even harder to remove ( Monmouth County SPCA )

open image in gallery A contractor had to come remove the shed's floorboards for rescuers to safely remove the animal ( Monmouth County SPCA )

It’s not illegal to own a Burmese python in New Jersey, but the animals do require a permit. Officials suspect the snake may have been released by someone who didn’t have one, or by an owner who simply couldn’t handle the snake after it grew too large.

Animal control officers arrived expecting to pull the snake back through the opening it used to crawl under the shed.

But there was a problem: the python recently ate a substantial meal, leaving it with a large and full belly.

With the python’s bulging abdomen blocking the way, rescuers couldn’t simply pull it out without risking injury.

The Daleys called in a contractor friend, who tore up the shed floor to give rescuers access from above.

But even with the floorboards gone, the python’s latest feast was still standing in the way.

“So we had to dig around him a little bit to free him up,” Crawford said. “Still couldn't tell exactly where his head was.”

open image in gallery X-rays revealed that the snake recently ate an opossum for dinner ( Monmouth County SPCA )

Eventually, the team managed to get the massive reptile out from beneath the shed. The Monmouth County SPCA’s medical staff performed X-rays on the snake to determine what was inside its stomach and make sure its recent meal had not caused any complications.

The images revealed the answer: an opossum.

Fortunately for the family, the python did not eat someone’s pet, which Crawford said could’ve been a real possibility for a snake that size.

The snake will eventually be placed in a zoo or transferred to a private owner with the proper expertise and permits to care for it.

“I’m not a big snake person myself,” Ed Daley told ABC 7.
