World.title: Belarus joins Russia’s war on freedom of information
World.content:
Belarus' decision to ban the Euronews website by designating it as “extremist” and adding it to its “Republican List of Extremist Materials” marks a new escalation by authorities in Minsk in their crackdown on independent media and free speech.

 

The Belarus Ministry of Information’s move, reported by Belarus-based media, resulted in the immediate restriction of access to Euronews’ digital platforms in the country’s territory, as shown by Euronews’ real-time traffic-monitoring systems.

As of Saturday, Belarus has still not communicated its decision to Euronews, which was reportedly taken on 4 August - nor has it outlined the reasoning behind it.

The Ministry of Information had already banned Euronews’ television broadcasts in April 2021 following its coverage of nationwide protests against Belarusian leader Aliaksandr Lukashenka.

Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko speaks to journalists during a joint press conference with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto at Merdeka Palace in Jakarta. AP Photo

The Belarus government's official argument then was that Euronews’ broadcasting license had expired and that the channel was publishing adverts in English rather than translating them into Russian or Belarusian in line with local laws.

Euronews was also not notified of that decision and once again learned of the ban through media outlets in Belarus.

In a statement published after the 2021 ban came into effect, Euronews condemned the decision and said that it would "do its utmost to ensure that its audiences in Belarus can very soon again have access, on television, to its hallmark impartial and quality journalism."

"In the meantime, these audiences will be able to continue following us on our digital platforms," it added.

Following in Russia's footsteps

Euronews had built a significant audience in Belarus and in Russia over the years, its digital traffic data shows.

However, Moscow decided to ban Euronews’ television and digital platforms across Russia in March 2022, shortly after it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as Euronews refused to comply with the censorship and propaganda-driven measures imposed by the Kremlin on the media.

Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister - Presidential Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev at the Kremlin in Moscow. Sputnik

The decision to stop broadcasting Euronews was taken by Russia’s audio-visual regulator Roskomnadzor following a request from the Prosecutor General’s Office. It threatened Euronews with “criminal liability” and accused the outlet of publishing “unreliable information on a special military operation being carried out by the Russian Armed Forces, as well as information containing calls for people to participate in mass (public) events.”

After Russian President Vladimir Putin's troops invaded Ukraine, the Kremlin told the media not to call its full-scale invasion a war, while also issuing other directives that contravened Euronews’ fundamental editorial values.

Responding at the time, Euronews rejected “the allegations of 'fake news' and of calling citizens to protest”.

“We firmly condemn this intolerable restriction imposed on the millions of people across Russia who relied on Euronews, more than ever, to get impartial fact-based news, in a context of heightened disinformation and propaganda,” Euronews said in a statement.

Russian authorities continued to criminalise the dissemination of what it called information “discrediting” the Russian army and threatened journalists with up to 15 years in prison.

More recently, Euronews revealed that multiple fake news videos were being posted on Russian social media copying the publication's journalistic and visual style in an attempt to spread false political information.

These come as part of a wider, sophisticated fake news campaign targeting Western media and European societies.

Belarus, Russia and Iran’s media crackdown

Minsk's decision mirrors a series of similar measures taken by Moscow in clamping down on internet platforms it does not fully control.

On the same day that Belarus took the decision to ban Euronews’ digital platforms, the Kremlin blocked dozens of VPN services used by Russians to bypass internet restrictions in a move that experts described as one of the largest crackdowns on VPN services in recent years.

The latest VPN blockade comes as Russia has been imposing constant restrictions on media outlets, social media and foreign technology companies ever since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In July 2025, Russia imposed a new legislation criminalising "searching for extremist content online", marking the first time Moscow hit internet users for consuming and distributing content deemed as banned in further crackdown on dissent and independent journalism.

Belarus’ decision to classify Euronews’ journalism as “extremist” appears to match this Russian legislation.

Then in August 2025, Russian authorities announced they were “partially” restricting calls through Telegram and WhatsApp messaging applications, in a further effort to tighten control over the internet and since the beginning of 2026 the Kremlin moved to fully block Telegram and WhatsApp everywhere across the country, triggering the largest wave of criticism from Kremlin supporters against the authorities in four years since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Iranian regime followed Russia and Belarus’ method to eliminate any outside information reaching their societies by bluntly blocking all internet access across Iran when it cracked down on the massive anti-regime protests in January 2026 and continued maintaining the internet ban throughout the Iran war.

Over the last months, the Tehran regime also imposed further measures of internet control and severe penalties on VPN usage, while designating selected medias as enemies of the state.

World.title: Tisza Party group nominates András Baka for new Hungarian president
World.content:
András Baka is an internationally recognised legal scholar, who began his career at the Institute for Legal Studies of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, then became director general of the College of Public Administration. The peak of his international judicial career came when he served for two terms, between 1991 and 2008, as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in Strasbourg. On his return home, in 2009, parliament elected him president of the Supreme Court. The second Orbán government, which came to power in 2010 with a constitution-making majority, removed him by renaming the Supreme Court as the Curia, thereby formally creating a new institution and appointing a new head to lead it.

 

Baka subsequently won a case against the Hungarian state at the European Court of Human Rights, which found that his rights to a fair trial and to freedom of expression had been violated. He has been a regular voice on rule-of-law issues in Hungary and abroad. He is an independent-minded, somewhat old-school lawyer, and Hungary has had several presidents of this type. His ability to embody national unity may be complicated by the fact that he has been an outspoken critic of the Orbán system both at home and internationally.

Powerless presidents instead of symbols of national unity

Before the elections, Tisza Party leader Péter Magyar had already indicated that, if they secured a constitution-making majority, they would remove most of the high public dignitaries appointed by Fidesz, with the exception of central bank governor Mihály Varga. He argued that these dignitaries were loyal Fidesz party foot soldiers who had failed to fulfil their constitutional duties and whose aim after the election would be to obstruct the work of the Tisza government.

In the Hungarian system the president of the republic primarily plays a ceremonial role and has little independent political room for manoeuvre. Under Fidesz rule, however, the presidents did not use even this limited legal and communicative space, instead operating in parallel with the government and cooperating with it in every respect.

During the period of government from 2010 to 2016, only János Áder, a political veteran of the party, managed to serve the two terms available to him in full.

László Sólyom, who had been elevated to the post by Fidesz while it was still in opposition and who projected an independent political and legal profile, was not elected for a second term. His successor, Pál Schmitt, a former Fidesz vice president, fell over a plagiarism scandal. János Áder then became president, and after his second term he was followed by Katalin Novák.

Novák spent her entire political career in Fidesz, but as a young woman she was officially meant to show a more European, more Western-facing face of the party than the mainstream led by Viktor Orbán. She had to step down after the pardon for sex abuse scandal. At that point Tamás Sulyok was elected, a figure little known to the public and without a strong public profile, and he too did not complete his first term.

President Tamás Sulyok was ultimately removed by means of a short sentence inserted into the 17th constitutional amendment, which the lawyer elected by Fidesz signed, thereby ending his mandate.

Tisza has indicated that it will adopt a new constitution within this parliamentary term and will at least consider the possibility of electing the president of the republic directly.

Tisza's first political misstep

Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised public consultation on the choice of president, then, after a very short time, announced that the parliamentary group was nominating women's world chess champion Judit Polgár. The announcement was followed by a strong outcry; critics of the decision argued that the absence of consultation cast a shadow over the selection process. Sensing the outrage, Polgár declined Magyar's offer. After the failed nomination, Medián, one of Hungary's most trusted pollsters, measured the first significant drop (3–5 percentage points) in support for Tisza, which nevertheless remained at a historically high level, at 68% among decided party voters.

Tisza chose Baka from three candidates; the other two were historian Ignác Romsics and independent lawyer Botond Fülöp, who publishes under the pseudonym Vidéki Prókátor and was the one who brought to light the pardon case that led to President Katalin Novák's resignation.

World.title: Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy
World.content:
The launch of the Yeni Party in Turkey promises to energise the country's struggling opposition. But while some polls show it leading, it remains vulnerable – already beset by arrests it says are "politically motivated".

Advertising

In a glitzy video, set to pumping music and shared widely across social media, Ozgur Ozel launched the Yeni Party – "New Party" – vowing to usher in a new era in Turkish politics and end President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s long rule.

Ozel founded the New Party after a court removed him from leading the main opposition party, the Republican People’s Party (CHP).

His rival, former party leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu, 77, who lost every election during his decade in charge of the CHP, replaced him.

Many in the country believe Erdogan played a role in the removal of Ozel, as his popularity grew thanks to tireless campaigning.

Riding the wave

The New Party is settings its sights beyond the CHP’s usual supporters.

"It covers the whole political spectrum in Turkish political life," explains Ozel's advisor Ilham Uzel.

"There are critical elements like democratisation, rule of law, secularism and a pro-Western approach, so we maintain these main pillars. But it is not confined to social democracy; we reach out to every section of Turkish society, including Islamists and conservatives, nationalists and liberals. We have Kurdish supporters."

The New Party is riding a wave of excitement. Ninety-one out of 135 CHP parliamentary deputies have defected to its ranks, joined by dozens of mayors and it is swiftly becoming the main opposition in parliament.

Turkey opposition worries that Europe is sacrificing democracy for security

Some polls show the party soaring above 30 percent, leaving Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party behind, while the CHP’s support has collapsed.

The New Party’s broad approach is finding fertile ground. "Even those who still support the governing coalition, the AK Party and MHP, are unhappy with how things are or how politics is practised, especially regarding economic issues. So there is a push towards change," says political commentator Sezin Oney.

"There is a yearning to change things at the grassroots, and the New Party may be the only party that can represent a new way of doing politics. But they have to live up to it, of course."

Corruption charges

Erdogan has remained in power for more than 20 years partly by exploiting divisions within the opposition, which is made up of conservatives, hardline secularists, and both Kurdish and Turkish nationalists.

The New Party has a key advantage over the strongly secular CHP, whose history is linked to past policies targeting Turkey’s large Kurdish minority and religious conservatives.

"CHP is identified with many bad experiences that the Kurds and conservative people had in past decades," said Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

"If you look at what Ozgur Ozel says during his speeches, you may clearly see the Yeni Party doesn’t have the baggage of CHP."

Erdogan has also often exploited the CHP’s history, painting it as anti-religious and hostile to Kurdish minority rights. The New Party faces the tricky task of keeping CHP loyalists on board while reaching new supporters.

But for now, simply staying out of jail may be the most pressing concern for its representatives.

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Several mayors who joined the New Party have been arrested on corruption charges, widely seen as politically motivated. In the past two years, 26 opposition mayors and hundreds of officials have been imprisoned on corruption allegations, compared to two mayors from Erdogan’s AK Party.

"They are cracking down on our party – every other day, mayors are arrested," says Uzgel. "They filed another charge against our leader. Nobody is safe in this authoritarian regime. So Mr Ozel is on the spot, definitely."

Ozel is protected by parliamentary immunity, but Oney warns he may be running out of time.

"Ozgur Ozel might be imprisoned himself once his immunity is removed by a parliamentary vote, that's a possibility. The only immunity he can have is the immunity bestowed upon him by the people. So only public opinion is protecting him. How much can it protect him? We'll see."

With parliament about to break for summer until October, Ozel has a brief window to strengthen his party and rally public support.

World.title: Kosovo PM Kurti egged in parliament amid political crisis
World.content:
Kosovo has held three elections in over two years. Albin Kurti's ruling Vetevendosje is struggling to garner the two-thirds majority required to elect a president.

Kosovo's parliament was suspended on Saturday after an opposition lawmaker threw eggs at caretaker Prime Minister Albin Kurti.

"Shame on you!" Time Kadrijaj of the conservative opposition Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) party shouted in parliament before hurling eggs at Kurti.

In response, Kurti said that he was "happy to pay this price" if it was the cost of dialogue.

Kurti's left-wing Vetevendosje (VV) party is known for its own parliamentary disruptions, with party representatives launching tear gas in the chamber in 2018 and also on multiple occasions in 2015.

Kadrijaj's AAK has seven seats in parliament, making it the fourth-largest opposition group Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS

What is the political situation in Kosovo?

The incident comes after days of negotiations as Kurti attempts to gain enough opposition support to elect a new president amid Kosovo's broader political crisis.

The Balkan country has held three elections in over two years.

Kurti achieved his parliamentary majority with ethnic minority MPs in a December election that followed an inconclusive vote in February 2025.

His VV party's share of the vote fell from 51% to 43% in a snap election in June, but it maintained a parliamentary majority alongside ethnic minority allies.

However, Kurti requires a two-thirds majority in parliament to elect a president.

The current negotiations seem to have ground to another stalemate, with neither side having agreed to a candidate.

A constitutional deadline to elect a speaker of parliament expired on Friday. Opposition lawmakers have threatened legal action over Kurti's request for more time to negotiate.

Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008 after the 1998-99 war, which ended with Serbia's withdrawal following a NATO bombing campaign.

Kosovo has been recognized by over half of the world's countries, including the United States and most European Union countries.

Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia.

World.title: Thousands attend Prague Pride parade
World.content:
Participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the CSD parade in Berlin. The march was accompanied by enhanced security measures.

Tens of thousands of people marched through Czech capital of Prague on Saturday as part of LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations.

The festival is to last for a week. The theme of this year's event is "Times are changing."

At the start of the parade, participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the Cristopher Street Day (CSD) parade in Berlin two weeks ago.

The July 25 attack killed one person and injured around 31 others.

Police said hundreds of officers were deployed to secure the parade route and added there were no major incidents Image: Ondrej Deml/CTK Photo/IMAGO

The Saturday march in Prague was accompanied by enhanced security measures, including the deployment of hundreds of police officers and a de-escalation team.

Participants were also told to carry banners by hand or to use plastic poles rather than wooden poles.

"As every year, the aim of the festival is to raise awareness of LGBT+ issues, to show how this community lives in the Czech Republic and that it is still waiting for equal rights," the director of Prague Pride, Kamila Frohlichova, was cited by Germany's DPA news agency as saying.

Marchers in Prague paid their respects to the victims of a car ramming in Berlin in late July Image: Michal Cizek/AFP

What else do we know about the Pride march in Prague?

According to police reports, there were no major incidents.

A group of counter-demonstrators also gathered along part of the march's trajectory.

The march began at Wenceslas Square in central Prague around noon (10:00 UTC/GMT) and arrived at Stvanice island in the Vltava River that passes through the city at around 2:30 p.m. local time, according to Czech media.

A musical program was held once the march reached its terminus and the festivities continued into the night.

World.title: US Senate confirms Trump loyalist Todd Blanche as new AG
World.content:
Republicans dropped their opposition and confirmed President Donald Trump's former defense lawyer to a Cabinet position. Now, Todd Blanche will act as the nation's top law enforcement officer.

The US Senate has narrowly approved President Donald Trump's nominee for the job of attorney general, making Todd Blanche the nation's top law enforcement officer in an early morning vote on Saturday.

The Republican-controlled body delivered a 50-49 vote to confirm the controversial Trump loyalist.

Louisiana Republican Bill Cassidy was the last-minute convert this time, supplying the crucial deciding vote after his colleagues Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine jumped ship to join the chamber's Democrats in voting against Blanche's appointment.

In explaining her opposition, Murkowski said the country was in need of an attorney general "who will check the worst impulses of this administration."

On the Senate floor, Cassidy outlined his own conversion, saying he believed Blanche's relationship with Trump would make him effective at pushing back against Trump's demands.

Blanche, a former federal prosecutor who was Trump's personal defense lawyer and had been serving as acting attorney general since April, wrote on X, "I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation's 88th attorney general."

Senators question whether Blanche will be nation's lawyer, or Trump's

There is great concern that Trump sees Blanche as "his lawyer," something that he has often openly expressed the need for in the position of attorney general, which is supposed to be independent.

"The attorney general is supposed to be the people's lawyer," Illinois Democratic Senator Dick Durbin said during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday.

"Mr. Blanche," added Durbin, the Committee's ranking Democrat, "continues to operate as the president's personal lawyer, treating the Justice Department like a law firm serving one client — the president."

On Saturday, Durbin said it would be a "serious mistake" to give Blanche control at the DOJ, "If there is ever a moment in history when we need an attorney general above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it's right now."

During his time in office, Trump has often railed against attorneys general for not being aggressive enough in pursuing his agenda — most often when it is tied to retribution against his political opponents.

Jeff Sessions, Bill Barr and Pam Bondi all fell out of the president's good graces for failing to fully satisfy his legal desires.

Blanche is seen as a staunch ally who has no qualms doing the president's bidding.

Epstein files: Expert warns release may shield 'Trump camp' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Blanche won votes by promising to scrap '1776 fund' and Trump tax immunity scheme

Blanche previously defended Trump against criminal charges over the falsification of business records with the intent of hiding an affair with an adult movie actress, as well as another for the mishandling of classified documents in his attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

Both cases were dropped after Trump won reelection in 2024.

Blanche's visibility rose when he defended Trump in a so-called 'hush-money trial' centered on his falsification of business records to hide an affair Image: Sarah Yenesel/Pool/REUTERS

During his time at the DOJ, Blanche has handled portions of the case against deceased sex offender and presidential friend Jeffrey Epstein — most prominently overseeing the release of millions of documents tied to the case, as well as the transfer of Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell to a more comfortable, minimum-security federal prison in Texas after he personally met with her.

Under Blanche and his predecessor Bondi, the DOJ has lost thousands of employees through firing, resignation or voluntary departure.

Blanche's candidacy was vehemently opposed by Democrats, and even some Republican lawmakers had qualms with his avoidance of forthright answers about a dubious $1.776 billion (€1.5 billion) compensation fund for presidential political allies — including those who stormed the US Capital on January 6, 2021 — accusing the federal government of unfair treatment; and DOJ directives that would see the president, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization shielded from tax audits and penalties for life.

Two retiring Republican senators, John Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (North Carolina), had loudly proclaimed that they would vote against Blanche's appointment unless the compensation fund was dropped.

He assured them that it would be, while also saying that the Trumps' tax immunity would only be applied "retroactively" and not to future filings, clearing the way for Saturday's confirmation vote.

World.title: Ukraine: Russia pounds Kyiv as Zelenskyy visits Serbia
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is visiting Serbia, a country that has traditionally been friendly with Moscow, as Russia strikes the Kyiv region once again.

As Russia continues its relentless bombardment of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is making his first visit to Serbia, a European country that has maintained friendly relations with Russia despite the latter's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Zelenskyy arrived in Belgrade Friday evening and had dinner with his Serbian counterpart, Aleksandar Vucic. They met again for talks at the presidential palace on Saturday.

Later, Zelenskyy wrote on X that he and Vucic had discussed ways to strengthen infrastructure in both countries, including ports and railways, as well as economic development, reconstruction, and job creation in Ukraine and Serbia.

Representatives from both countries signed a memorandum of understanding regarding agricultural and food safety cooperation.

Zelenskyy added that the leaders also discussed the challenges of the upcoming winter in Ukraine, heavily hit by ⁠Russian attacks on energy facilities, and relations with the European Union. He also thanked Vucic for a new package of humanitarian support for Ukraine.

Serbia supports Ukraine's territorial integrity

Vucic said that Serbia will continue to support Ukraine's independence and territorial integrity, including the territories that Russia has seized since 2014.

"You have never heard a single bad word about our country, not from Volodymyr Zelenskyy nor anyone else in Ukraine, and I am extremely grateful to our Ukrainian friends for that," Vucic said.

The remark appeared to address the fact that Ukraine refuses to recognize Kosovo's independence, which was declared in 2008. Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia.

Vucic said he was skeptical that either Serbia or Ukraine would quickly join the European Union. However, he added that Belgrade would support Kyiv's bid.

Serbia has repeatedly refused to put sanctions on Moscow. This has angered the EU and delayed Belgrade's path to joining the bloc.

Both leaders also said their countries want to improve economic cooperation and finalize a free trade agreement by the end of the year. ​

Despite its dependence on Russian energy, Serbia has supplied nonmilitary aid to Ukraine. The Kremlin has accused Serbian firms of selling munitions to Ukraine, but Vucic has denied this claim.

Vucic traveled to Ukraine for a regional summit in 2025 and again this year. Despite pledging aid to Ukraine, he has refrained from signing a formal declaration of support for Ukraine in the war.

Russian attacks on Kyiv continue while Kyiv strikes Russian refineries

The meeting came after at least four people, including a child, were killed in overnight Russian air attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, and the surrounding region, officials said on Saturday.

"Last night, Russia killed three people in Pukhivka, Kyiv region, with drone strikes," Zelenskyy wrote on X. He added that the victims were a grandfather, a grandmother and their 3-year-old grandson.

Authorities said three other members of the family and a neighbor who came to their aid were hospitalized.

Ukraine faces Patriot missile shortage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At least one more person was killed in Kyiv in a strike involving six ballistic missiles against civilian infrastructure, according to Zelenskyy.

Ukraine's air force reported downing or intercepting 135 of the 151 drones that Russia launched overnight.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's General Staff announced that the military had attacked Russia's Ilsky and Syzran oil refineries overnight, resulting in fires at both locations.

World.title: Iran war: IRGC says Hormuz to open if US accepts Iran's terms
World.content:
Skip next section What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

08/08/2026 August 8, 2026 What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

Earlier, we reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said talks with the US on reopening the Strait of Hormuz depend on Washington "compensating" Iran for the US "violation" of a June memorandum of understanding the two nations signed.

Aragchi and the IRGC had also pointed to "other conditions" that would need to be met.

Iran's Supreme National Security Council said the country would not lift its blockade of Hormuz until the US "corrects its behavior."

In a statement by the council's secretary and Revolutionary Guard commander Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr that was published on Iran's state broadcaster, Iran said the US must:

Never threaten Iran again

Permanently end its war against Iran and its allies in the region, namely Lebanese militants Hezbollah; Houthi rebels in Yemen; and Hamas in the Gaza Strip

Lift its blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz and pull its military out of the area

Lift sanctions and release frozen Iranian assets

The US has yet to respond.

World.title: War, terror, diplomacy: What if Israel takes Al-Aqsa Mosque?
World.content:
Reports from Jerusalem suggest that Israeli authorities are taking over one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. If they do, experts say anything could happen, from war to terrorism to ending diplomatic ties.

The statement issued after this week's meeting in Jordan was blunt about what might happen next.

Israeli infringements on one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque in east Jerusalem, could lead to "a religious conflict with repercussions that will extend beyond the region and threaten regional and international peace and security," the foreign ministers of 10 countries belonging to the Arab League said after Wednesday's emergency meeting in Amman, Jordan. The statement was also signed by ministers from Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, and Malaysia.

Jordan's foreign minister called the meeting because of mounting evidence that the Israeli government is surreptitiously changing a decades-old agreement meant to ensure intercommunal peace at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, an area of great religious significance to Muslims, Jews, and Christians.

"We warn that tampering with the status quo … could trigger a religious conflict that will reverberate beyond Palestine and Jordan into the whole Muslim world," Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi told the UK newspaper the Guardian before the meeting.

Israel's Foreign Ministry issued a response, saying the statement was inaccurate and Jerusalem "has never been more open and accessible to worshippers of all faiths."

Jews at Al-Aqsa: In 2015, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said 'Muslims pray on the Temple Mount, non-Muslims visit the Temple Mount' Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

Why is Al-Aqsa such a big issue?

Al-Aqsa is considered the third-holiest site in Islam, after Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia. The compound, also known as the Temple Mount, is also Judaism's holiest site — two Jewish temples are thought to have stood there — and it is also of significance to Christians for its biblical connections to Jesus Christ's life.

Al-Aqsa also bears a lot of political weight because the mosque is seen by many as the embodiment of Palestinian identity, a flashpoint in a city sought as the capital of any eventual Palestinian state.

Because of the site's importance, when Israel first occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, it was deemed in the interests of Israeli national security to keep allowing Muslims to worship there. Jews could only visit and would not be allowed to pray there. Instead Jewish visitors perform religious rituals at the wall below the mosque, known as the Western or Wailing Wall.

Jordan was also allowed to continue its century-old custodianship of the site, and today the mosque is administered by a religious trust called the Islamic Waqf, paid for by Jordan at about $20 million (€17 million) annually. Israeli authorities still take care of security there.

Muslims say the Prophet Muhammad ascended to heaven from Al-Aqsa Image: Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo/picture alliance

This delicate compromise is known as the "status quo." But recent reports indicate that the situation has been changing.

Residents of Jerusalem say dozens of mosque officials employed by Jordan have been prevented from entering Al-Aqsa this year.

The number of Muslim worshipers halved during 2025 , according to Jerusalem-based monitors. More Jewish worshipers are being allowed in and are increasingly overtly performing rituals, something forbidden for decades, including by Jewish religious authorities. The Times of Israel reported in January that police openly let Jewish visitors take printed prayer sheets onto the site for the first time.

In June, there were also reports of an Israeli-US plan to turn the mosque area into a "multifaith center," although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later denied any knowledge of such a plan.

Why is this happening now?

This is not the first time that the governments of Muslim-majority countries and activists in Jerusalem have issued such warnings.

For decades, Jewish fringe groups, often referred to as the Temple Mount movement, have demanded that they be allowed to pray at the site. The most extremist of these groups say they want to demolish the mosque and construct a new Jewish temple.

At first they were mostly ignored, Jerusalem-based lawyer Daniel Seidemann wrote in 2025 . Seidemann is the founder of Terrestrial Jerusalem, an organization that tracks such developments in the city. But, he said, that "radical fringe" has become more mainstream. "Over time, the Temple Mount movements, backed by more than 100 rabbis associated with the settler movement in the West Bank, became more visible, more vocal and more provocative," Seidemann said.

"This crisis has been decades in the making," said Omar Rahman, a fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. "There's been an effort from religious extremists to destroy the Al-Aqsa Mosque since at least the 1980s, when plots to do that were uncovered. But those groups and those ideologies have gained more representation within the Israeli [parliament] Knesset today."

In July, thousands of Jews prayed at the Al-Aqsa compound in violation of the status quo agreement Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

An October 2025 report by the Ir Amim Association , which focuses on Israeli-Palestinian issues in Jerusalem, found that politicians, including from within Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's national-conservative Likud party, frequently break rules around the Al-Aqsa status quo but never face consequences from authorities.

"In practice, Netanyahu allows and normalizes grave breaches of the status quo," the association reported. Yet Netanyahu "continues to declare that his government remains committed to the status quo and nothing has changed."

What happens if erosion of Al Aqsa status quo continues?

"It would be very unwise to make any sort of prediction," Joost Hiltermann, a special adviser for the Middle East and North Africa at the Crisis Group think tank, told DW.

But, Hiltermann said, it's essential to consider that "while the fate of Jerusalem as a city may be an overriding Palestinian concern, the fate of the holy sites of Islam in Jerusalem is an abiding global Muslim concern. Not just for the Arab world but also for the largest Muslim countries: Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh. So any Israeli attempt to change the status quo would face a global backlash."

In the past, changes have led to violence. In 2000, Ariel Sharon, an Israeli right-wing opposition leader at the time, visited Al-Aqsa — an event that was seen as one reason for the Palestinian uprising known as the Second Intifada. In 2017, when Israeli authorities erected cameras and metal detectors at the site, it led to deadly protests.

UNESCO has declared the Old City of Jerusalem, including the Temple Mount, a World Heritage site, so any changes could be interpreted as a breach of international law, observers say Image: Simon Beni/Middle East Images/picture alliance

One likely outcome of further infringements of the status quo would be major public protests in Muslim-majority countries. "While the Arab regimes would be reluctant to engage in any sort of confrontation with Israel, their publics will be outraged," Hiltermann said. "The regimes will have to manage that, and they will try to do so by launching vigorous criticism of Israel, not followed by any action — they've become very good at that. The same will be true for Indonesia and others. But all of them may have a hard time controlling domestic fury."

Rahman said the consequences of further Israeli infringement would depend on how radically things changed at Al-Aqsa. "It would trigger a fairly significant reaction, but the extent of it is hard to say," he said. "It could spark a catastrophic religious war or maybe just a diplomatic reaction, or maybe it simply adds to the well of grievance against Israel," he added.

Because Al Aqsa is so important in Islam, it could also make it hard for some countries to resist an upsurge in anti-Israel feeling, even if they might want to, he adds. For example, countries like Morocco and the United Arab Emirates that normalized relations with Israel might feel forced to reverse that.

Because of Al Aqsa's significance to Palestinian identity, the Gaza-based militant group Hamas often says it is defending the mosque. Extremist groups with an Islamist background have also used defense of Al Aqsa to recruit members.

Edited by: M Gagnon

World.title: Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border
World.content:
A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said. Bulgaria summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for consultations.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said that a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace from the north and exploded near the Romanian border on Saturday morning.

According to the prime minister, there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, as the drone exploded in a sunflower field 100 meters from the border with Romania. He noted that neither of the two neighboring countries had detected the drone.

Radev added that the incident occurred about 1,000 meters from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine.

"We will continue to monitor the situation and strengthen surveillance. Following this incident, we will also redeploy border police anti-drone detection and countermeasure capabilities from the border with Turkey to the border with Romania," Radev said.

What do we know about the drone?

Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his Cabinet's security council, Radev did not specify where the drone came from or what type it was.

However, he said it was believed the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives given the strength of the blast and the black smoke it produced.

When asked if the drone was civilian or military, Radev said that there was photographic evidence available. However, because the drone was damaged in the explosion, it was impossible to determine its type.

After analysing the debris, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was of a type "widely used by the Ukrainian military." According to the AFP news agency, Bulgaria also summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for consultations.

Kyiv said it was "in close contact with the Bulgarian side to clarify the circumstances" of the incident, the latest case of a drone straying into NATO airspace as Ukraine fights off Russia's invasion.

"We can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria," Ukraine's foreign ministry spokesman Georgiy Tykhyi said.

Radev said the drone was not detected in Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size.

Russian drone hits Romanian apartment block To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Drone incidents on rise in EU countries

In recent months, there have been an increasing number of incidents involving drones in Eastern European countries that are both EU and NATO members and that support Ukraine in its four-and-a-half-year war against Russia's invasion.

The origin of the drone that exploded in Bulgaria and its potential connection to Russia or Ukraine are still unclear. Radev said that teams from the Bulgarian border police and the Ministry of Defense are working to determine the origin of the drone.

Bulgaria's Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said the incident would be raised at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council early next week.

Romania, which borders Ukraine, has faced frequent drone incursions, including crashes on its territory, such as a May incident in which a drone struck an apartment building.

Earlier this week in Germany, an explosive-laden drone was defused at Leipzig Airport, in what Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called a "new level of danger."

World.title: EU holds talks with big tech over Ceuta misinformation
World.content:
EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen has called for closer monitoring of social media platforms moving forward, amid the spread of misinformation during the recent migrant influx at Spain's Ceuta.

EU Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy Henna Virkkunen has called on social media giants to exercise closer monitoring of their platforms for misinformation, especially "during crisis situations."

Virkkunen was referring to last week's Ceuta border crisis, which European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities say was exacerbated by the spread of misinformation on social media, including TikTok, Telegram and Meta platforms.

Commissioner Virkkunen addressed the disinformation on social media, calling for greater EU monitoring of platforms during crisis situations.

"Platforms must act decisively in keeping the integrity of the digital space, in particular during crisis situations," she wrote on X.

"Monitoring must increase, cooperation with fact-checkers to be strengthened," Virkkunen wrote after a Friday meeting with representatives from TikTok and Meta — which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

Social media increasingly central to 'political debate'

A number of the estimated 72,000 people who stormed Ceuta from Morocco said they were attracted by false promises disseminated on social media and that they were lied to about the situation.

Spain and Morocco have also exchanged blame, with authorities in Rabat blaming a Spanish Supreme Court ruling that it says was exploited by human traffickers and misrepresented on social media.

Madrid says Morocco should have done a better job at stopping the tens of thousands of migrants who crossed the border.

Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the end, Spanish authorities say 80 people were killed during the course of events.

Moroccan authorities reported that 11 people died on their side of the border.

Rights groups estimate the total number of dead at more than 140.

The situation in Ceuta and the circumstances surrounding it have added more fuel to Europe's ongoing political fight over issues related to immigration and security.

Did misinformation on social media cause the Ceuta crisis?

In Ceuta, migrants pointed to social media messages and videos announcing that the EU border at Ceuta was suddenly open.

World.title: Primer día de control a los viajeros procedentes de Italia: la policía pide la documentación a solo el 5% o 10% de los pasajeros
World.content:
Desde este sábado, un centenar de agentes de la Policía Nacional participa en los controles fronterizos establecidos para los viajeros procedentes de Italia, según fuentes del Ministerio del Interior. El despliegue deriva de la decisión del Gobierno, adoptada a última hora de la tarde del viernes, de restablecer temporalmente los controles en aeropuertos y puertos españoles con conexiones directas con el país transalpino. La medida entró en vigor a las 00.00 de este sábado y se mantendrá, inicialmente, hasta la misma hora del próximo 7 de septiembre, aunque el plazo podrá modificarse en función de la evolución de la situación.

Según datos facilitados por el Ministerio del Interior, correspondientes al periodo comprendido entre 00,01 y las 21.00 horas de este sábado, la Policía Nacional ha controlado a un total de 199 viajeros nacionales de terceros países llegados a España en 12 vuelos procedentes de Italia, informa Efe. Los controles comenzaron a la medianoche en los aeropuertos Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas y Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat y se han extendido a lo largo de la jornada a Sevilla, Bilbao, Alicante y Valencia. Interior prevé ampliarlos también a los aeródromos de Baleares y Canarias.

España reestableció los registros fronterizos después de que el Gobierno de Giorgia Meloni rechazara levantar los que aplica desde el 1 de agosto a los viajeros procedentes de España, tras la entrada masiva de migrantes en Ceuta, un territorio que, no obstante, no pertenece en la práctica al espacio Schengen, porque a todos los viajeros que quieren ir de allí hacia la Península se les controla la documentación.

España ha notificado a la Comisión Europea la recuperación de estos controles, según confirman desde el Ejecutivo de la UE. La medida, al de forma imprevista, solo puede prolongarse durante un mes, y es prorrogable por otros dos, informa Manuel V. Gómez. El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, ha comunicado este sábado a las autoridades de la Unión Europea la decisión de restablecer los controles adoptada por el Gobierno. Marlaska ha informado a la vicepresidenta ejecutiva de la Comisión Europea, Henna Virkkunen, y al comisario europeo de Asuntos de Interior y Migración, Magnus Brunner. Además, se ha dirigido a la presidenta del Parlamento Europeo, Roberta Metsola, y a la secretaria general del Consejo de la UE, Thérèse Blanchet. En su escrito, el ministro justifica la medida por la evolución de la presión migratoria en la ruta del Mediterráneo central que afecta a Italia y por sus posibles repercusiones sobre “el orden público y la seguridad interior”, especialmente por la actividad de las redes de delincuencia transfronteriza vinculadas a la migración irregular.

Con todo, Bruselas confía en que Italia levante “pronto” los controles para los viajeros procedentes de España. El comisario de Interior de la Comisión Europea, Magnus Brunner, ve “señales de que Italia podría levantar pronto los controles” para viajeros procedentes de España. Lo ha afirmado en un mensaje en X después de hablar este sábado con los ministros de Interior español e italiano, Matteo Piantedosi. Esas señales el comisario austriaco las ve en las declaraciones del ministro transalpino señalando: “Espero, ante todo, que el día 15, o incluso antes, en cualquier momento, se resuelva el problema”. “He estado en contacto con los ministros español e italiano hoy. Ambos me han confirmado que los controles en las fronteras son temporales”, ha querido destacar el comisario Brunner en su mensaje, casi un día después que España anunciara que iba a recuperar los controles fronterizos para los viajeros que llegaran procedentes de Italia, sea en avión o en barco.

En España cada avión está siendo supervisado por entre dos y cuatro policías —en función de su número de pasajeros—, que comprueban de forma aleatoria la documentación de entre el 5% y el 10% del pasaje, según Interior. Esto supone una media de unas 15 personas controladas en los vuelos operados con aviones medianos y de unas 25 en los de mayor capacidad.

Un policía comprueba la documentación de un viajero de Italia, este sábado en el Prat. EFE

La Moncloa decidió elevar el tono ante Roma después de que el Ejecutivo de Meloni introdujera la semana pasada controles en frontera a los ciudadanos provenientes de España por la entrada masiva de inmigrantes en Ceuta. El Ejecutivo español respondió con dureza este viernes al Ejecutivo italiano y le advirtió de que, si no retiraba estas restricciones antes de que termine el domingo 9 de agosto, “España se verá obligada a adoptar medidas proporcionales para proteger los intereses y la dignidad de sus ciudadanos”, como finalmente ha ocurrido.

Entre los principales puntos de origen de los vuelos sometidos a estas comprobaciones se encuentran Fiumicino y Ciampino, en Roma; Malpensa, en Milán; Nápoles, Venecia y Florencia, pero la lista aumentará en los próximos días. En cuanto al tráfico marítimo, este sábado solo está prevista la llegada desde Italia de un crucero a la terminal del Puerto de Barcelona, donde se efectuarán controles igualmente aleatorios.

Dos modalidades de control

Los equipos encargados de los controles fronterizos a los viajeros procedentes de Italia están decidiendo sobre la marcha si realizan las comprobaciones a todos los pasajeros de un vuelo seleccionado de manera aleatoria o únicamente a determinadas personas dentro de un avión. “Funcionan las dos modalidades”, explican a EL PAÍS fuentes del Ministerio del Interior, que precisan que la elección depende en cada momento del equipo que esté al cargo del control.

Para hacer estas comprobaciones, los equipos disponen de la información del Registro de Nombres de los Pasajeros (PNR, por sus siglas en inglés), a través del cual las aerolíneas comunican con antelación los datos de los viajeros que transportan al país de destino. A partir de esa información, pueden optar por “elegir un vuelo” y controlar a todos sus pasajeros o seleccionar dentro de un avión a las personas a las que se realizará la comprobación, según las mismas fuentes.

Los controles fronterizos a los pasajeros de los vuelos procedentes de Italia se están realizando a la salida de la pasarela de acceso a la aeronave —el denominado finger—, sin desviar el flujo de viajeros hacia las zonas habituales de control de fronteras exteriores, según han explicado este sábado fuentes del Ministerio del Interior.

El número de policías de fronteras desplegados se adapta a la cantidad de pasajeros de cada vuelo y las comprobaciones se realizan de forma aleatoria, no sistemática, sobre ciudadanos de países que no pertenecen a la Unión Europea. Los agentes comprueban que estos viajeros cumplen los requisitos establecidos en el Código de Fronteras Schengen, como disponer de un pasaporte válido y, cuando sea necesario, de visado o tarjeta de residencia. Los ciudadanos de Estados miembros quedan exentos de estas inspecciones para agilizar la salida de los aviones. Cuando existen dudas sobre algún pasajero que requieren un examen más exhaustivo, este es trasladado al puesto fronterizo, donde se realizan las comprobaciones adicionales y, si procede, se tramita la denegación de entrada u otro procedimiento previsto por la normativa de extranjería.

Un pasajero: “Espero que acabe lo antes posible”

En el Aeropuerto del Prat, en Barcelona, los viajeros que no portaban el DNI consigo han sido llevados a una sala aparte para identificarlos. Giovanni (no da su apellido) ha subido la mañana de este sábado a un avión en Roma con destino al aeropuerto del Prat en Barcelona. “Al llegar, la policía nos ha dividido en dos grupos. A los italianos nos han pedido la documentación. Espero que esta situación acabe lo antes posible”, admitía un tanto molesto en la zona de salidas de la T1 del aeropuerto catalán.

Fuentes de la Policía Nacional en la infraestructura aeroportuaria barcelonesa aseguraban este sábado: “Italia es un país caliente en materia de inmigración. Solo revisaremos a los pasajeros que sospechemos que han subido en algún avión pero son de procedencia extracomunitaria y quieren acceder a España”.

En la práctica, los controles en Barcelona se han hecho de forma totalmente aleatoria, concentrándose en un vuelo procedente de Roma. De hecho, la normalidad imperaba esta mañana en el aeropuerto. Jorge Villoslada es español. Viaja muy a menudo y este sábado partió de Roma en dirección Barcelona. “Ha pasado algo muy raro. Al llegar, la policía nos ha preguntado qué hacíamos en España. Yo he enseñado mi DNI y me han dejado salir. A los que no tenían documentación española les han llevado a una sala para identificarles”, sostiene.

El vuelo procedente de Bolonia ha tenido mayor suerte en lo que a controles policiales se refiere. Libia (no da su apellido) es de Módena. Ha subido este sábado a un avión en Bolonia dirección a Barcelona. “Al llegar al Prat no hemos encontrado ningún control. Creo que el problema es más en Italia”. Nicoletta es de Turín y ha aterrizado en el mismo vuelo: “Hemos llegado con el carné de identidad en la mano por si había problemas, pero nadie ha dicho nada”.

Críticas en Italia

La oposición italiana ha criticado este sábado la decisión del Gobierno de Meloni de no levantar los controles en las fronteras marítimas y áreas con España, que impuso tras lo sucedido en Ceuta, al considerar que se ha creado “una crisis diplomática sin fundamento” y un perjuicio para sus ciudadanos. “La cínica propaganda del gobierno de Meloni ha producido lo que era previsible: un bumerán que los italianos pagarán caro”, ha explicado en una nota el líder de Alianza Verde e Izquierdas, Nicola Fratoiani, recoge Efe. Para Fratoiani, “se trata de un error garrafal y deberían detenerla de inmediato y retirar inmediatamente el disparate de la suspensión del Schengen”, especialmente después de que el Ejecutivo español introdujese desde la medianoche la misma medida. Para la diputada de la mayor formación en la oposición, el Partido Demócrata (Pd), Laura Boldrini, la jugada de Meloni “no podía haber salido peor”. “Esta vez, la crisis diplomática sin fundamento con España, provocada por el Gobierno de Meloni con el objetivo de hacer quedar en ridículo a España a nivel internacional, se ha convertido en un gol en propia puerta”, ha dicho Boldrini.

World.title: Xandra Falcó (Círculo Fortuny): “En España todavía hay cierto tabú para hablar de lujo y de dinero”
World.content:
Lleva seis años al frente de una asociación que trabaja para potenciar las marcas de alta gama españolas y resalta la importancia que el sector tiene en la economía. Trabaja para que la labor de los artesanos tenga más visibilidad

A Xandra Falcó no le importa decir su año de nacimiento, 1967. Todo lo contrario, se muestra contenta de soplar velas y disfrutar de la vida. No en vano, para ella el lujo es “el tiempo compartido alrededor de una mesa, o de una botella de vino, con familia y amigos”. Esta empresaria vitivinícola se puso al frente de Círcu­lo Fortuny, una organización sin ánimo de lucro para potenciar las marcas de lujo y alta gama españolas, hace seis años, tras fallecer su padre, Carlos Falcó, marqués de Griñón, impulsor y presidente de la asociación. Círculo Fortuny agrupa ahora a unas 80 firmas e instituciones de diversos sectores. Desde viajes a gastronomía, pasando por bodegas y museos. Sin olvidar los artesanos, uno de los colectivos en los que están más enfocados.

Pregunta: ¿Cómo se entra en Círculo Fortuny?

Respuesta: Es una asociación de marcas españolas reconocidas, independientemente del capital. Es decir, puede ser una firma como Loewe, que el capital es extranjero, pero la marca tiene que ser española. Hay que tener una trayectoria por lo menos de más de cinco años. La junta directiva vota la entrada o no. Además de eso, tenemos una serie de socios corporativos, referentes por distintos motivos. Como Iberia o El Corte Inglés, que es el mayor vendedor de productos de lujo de España. Y luego están los socios artesanos, que tienen una facturación más modesta, pero que a nosotros nos parece que la contribución es enorme. Porque que alguien como Felipe Conde o La Pajarita en Madrid formen parte de Círculo Fortuny con la trayectoria que tienen es importantísimo. Hay mucha sinergia entre las marcas, entre las grandes y las pequeñas en ese sentido.

P: ¿Qué les diferencia de otras asociaciones del sector del lujo?

R: Somos una asociación sin ánimo de lucro que defiende los intereses del sector. No nos metemos en eventos comerciales de ningún tipo. Lo que queremos defender es a las marcas españolas de excelencia cultural y creativa. La importancia que tienen, así como la contribución al empleo y el peso económico del sector.

P: ¿Considera que no se le da al sector del lujo la importancia que tiene por su peso en la economía, que se sigue viendo como algo frívolo?

R: Poco a poco se va entendiendo que el sector del lujo en Europa son 1.500 billones de euros de facturación, lo que supone un 4% del PIB europeo y casi el 11% de las exportaciones. Eso es una enorme contribución al motor económico de Europa. En España es más pequeño, y quizás se ve menos porque no tenemos marcas tan grandes como en otros países. Pero sí producimos para muchas de esas marcas. Eso contribuye a que se genere empleo muchas veces en territorios de lo que nosotros llamamos la España de las oportunidades.

P: ¿Cuál es la mayor diferencia que ha notado en el lujo español en estos seis años que lleva al frente de Círculo Fortuny?

R: Una de las grandes oportunidades para Círculo Fortuny es que, desde hace unos años, el lujo ha pasado de ser el producto, los bienes personales, la marroquinería, la moda, los bolsos, la joyería, a entrar en un mundo de experiencias mucho más amplio. En ese sentido, España tiene una oportunidad extraordinaria. El mundo de la experiencia ya es más del 50% de la facturación del sector del lujo, y yo creo que en nuestro país hay tantos lugares que pueden ofrecer esa excelencia... Es una enorme oportunidad para seguir creciendo y se está desarrollando.

P: ¿Ha cambiado la imagen que se tiene de España en el sector del lujo internacional?

R: Sin duda. Cada vez tenemos más turistas internacionales. Y se consolidan mercados que eran muy potentes en Francia o en Italia, como Estados Unidos, que es uno de que más crece en España. La llegada de las grandes hoteleras como Four Seasons, Mandarin Oriental o Rosewood hace que ese turista de repente tenga una marca conocida y que quiera aterrizar en España. Y esas compañías, al mismo tiempo, se han asociado con marcas españolas de referencia, como ha pasado con el Ritz o el Villa Magna, que han mantenido su nombre.

Xandra Falcó. Jaime Villanueva

P: La llegada de ese turismo de lujo hace que aumente el precio medio de las habitaciones. ¿Hay cierto riesgo de que al final el turismo se quede para una élite?

R: Había llegado el momento de poner un poquito de foco en ese turista que no llega con todo incluido, sino que viene y gasta en destino. Y eso es muy importante para las marcas locales. Un turista que paga a lo mejor dos veces más que antes en un hotel, también gasta en la restauración local, en el artesano de aquí, en buscar experiencias que son distintas. En los últimos estudios que hicimos, el turista de alto impacto se gasta en España hasta cuatro veces más por persona y día en destino que el turista medio. Pero es que la media en Europa es ocho veces más. Es un tipo de viajero que siempre va a ser una parte minoritaria, pero que el impacto en el destino, en los comercios y restaurantes locales es enorme. No podemos dejar de trabajar en él.

P: Sostienen en la asociación que este tipo de viajero ayuda a de­ses­tacionalizar el turismo y llevarlo a otras zonas del país, lo que ustedes llaman la España de las oportunidades.

R: Ahí queda muchísimo por desarrollar. Yo voy mucho a La Rioja y es un paisaje absolutamente extraordinario. Es una zona a desarrollar, al igual que ocurrió en otras europeas, como puede ser la Toscana o la Provenza, que quizá nos llevan todavía delantera. Y ahí hay proyectos increíbles como, por ejemplo, Abadía Retuerta Le Domaine, un lugar extraordinario que ha conseguido en unos años convertirse en destino. Los viajeros van ahí directamente para conocer el hotel, quedarse en una abadía, en un territorio y un paisaje único, rodeado de viñedos. En Sevilla parece que se está poniendo el foco también más. Y luego vendrán otros territorios, como ha sucedido en Francia o en Italia.

P: Habla de turistas de alto impacto, no usa el término ricos, ¿hay cierto tabú todavía en España para hablar de lujo y de dinero?

R: Sí, sí lo hay. Hay esa idea de que el lujo está asociado a precio. Hace poco leía una entrevista a Enrique Loewe en El País en la que hablaba de que el lujo es lo que brilla, pero también es la luz. El lujo tiene un precio alto, pero es una consecuencia, no es el objetivo. Un producto de lujo conlleva historia, talento, saber hacer, innovación. Hay muchas cosas que están detrás. Cuando visitas Cinco Jotas y ves el trabajo que hay para que un jamón salga al mercado, es que es enorme, y de repente no te parece caro. Cuando vas a una bodega y ves en los vinos top el trabajo en el viñedo, las barricas, las condiciones meteorológicas, el talento humano, todo lo que se hace para que un vino sea extraordinario, piensas en lo que vale y dices, pues tampoco es para tanto. O en un plato de cerámica, ese saber hacer de la pincelada, del trabajo bien hecho. Eso hay que valorarlo. Por el conocimiento, el talento, la creatividad, el diseño. Y además que esos productos son de unas tiradas muy cortas, no tienen la escala de las grandes producciones, lo que conlleva que tengan un precio a lo mejor más alto.

P: ¿En España no nos hemos sabido vender tan bien como otros países de nuestro entorno?

R: Cada vez menos, pero en este asunto había una asignatura ­pendiente. Porque a los propios españoles nos parece mejor siempre lo que viene de fuera. Eso está cambiando. Enormemente en el mundo del vino, sin duda, y en otros sectores también. Las nuevas generaciones están orgullosísimas de lo nuestro, de nuestras marcas, y esa es una de las ambiciones de Círculo Fortuny: decir que tenemos unos productos que son extraordinarios. En algunos casos puede faltar un poco trayectoria de marca, pero en calidad, en esencia, en talento están a la par que los italianos o los franceses. Los españoles tenemos que luchar por lo nuestro.

P: ¿Cuál es el principal problema al que se enfrenta la artesanía en España hoy en día?

R: Hay muchos. Uno, la visibilidad, la llegada al mercado. El cómo pasas de un taller pequeñito a que te conozca el gran público. Las herramientas como la IA hoy en día, en esa parte del negocio, te pueden ayudar muchísimo. Lo que intentamos con los premios Maestro Artesano, que hemos celebrado ya la quinta edición, es ayudar a visibilizar el talento. Hace 20 años, el mundo de los chefs, por ejemplo, no era tan glamuroso. Y hoy en día lo es. Pues esa es un poco nuestra misión. Que el prestigio del artesano vuelva a estar encima de la mesa, y que ese talento que ha estado durante siglos asociado al arte vuelva a tener su valor. El diálogo entre el artista y el artesano ha estado siempre en la historia de la pintura, de la escultura y de muchos de los oficios. Y de alguna manera, el artesano siempre ha estado un poco en la sombra. Nosotros queremos ponerlo en primer plano, porque su trabajo es fundamental.

P: ¿Y esa visibilidad puede ayudar a que más jóvenes se interesen por la artesanía?

R: Creo que sí. Pero todavía es mucho en el lado del artista, del diseñador, más que en el de las manos del artesano. Aunque está empezando a cambiar. Creo que entre la gente joven hay una vuelta atrás, a trabajar con las manos. A hacer algo de verdad. Estamos en esta era tecnológica, pero al mismo tiempo hay una cierta vocación a hacer algo manual.

World.title: Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate hit by data breach
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Football club Ajax, bank ING and eyewear chain Ace & Tate have been caught up in the data breach at logistics firm CEVA Logistics, which came to light this week when Bol and De Bijenkorf warned customers their details may have been exposed.

CEVA handles deliveries for the companies and had access to the customer data needed to fulfil orders. The firm says it cannot rule out that personal details were leaked, although the companies affected say no payment details, usernames or passwords were taken.

Whether addresses, email addresses or phone numbers were exposed remains unclear.

At ING, the breach affects customers who ordered physical products through the bank’s rewards points scheme.

Ajax has advised supporters to be extra alert to phishing messages in the coming weeks. The club and Ace & Tate have both reported the breach to privacy watchdog AP, as Bol did earlier this week.

Ace & Tate has warned customers that current orders may be delayed, although online ordering is still running. CEVA said it would respond to the breach at a later stage.

World.title: Actor Peter Faber, star of Dutch cinema’s golden age, dies at 82
World.content:
Peter Faber, one of the best-known faces of Dutch film and theatre for half a century, has died at the age of 82.

Faber was admitted to hospital in early July with breathing difficulties related to untreatable heart problems, his family told news agency ANP.

He broke through in the 1970s, widely regarded as the golden age of Dutch cinema, with roles in Keetje Tippel and Paul Verhoeven’s wartime classic Soldaat van Oranje – the film that later spawned the long-running musical which closed last month after 16 years.

He also took the title role in the 1976 film of Max Havelaar, Multatuli’s classic novel about Dutch colonial rule, and appeared alongside Sean Connery and Anthony Hopkins in Richard Attenborough’s A Bridge Too Far.

Faber began his career as a co-founder of Het Werkteater, an Amsterdam collective set up in the early 1970s to shake up Dutch theatre with performances about ordinary people and recognisable emotions. He won the Louis d’Or, the top Dutch theatre prize for a male actor, twice.

He kept working into his eighties. His final film role came in 2023 in Sweet Dreams, the Dutch entry for the 2024 Oscars, in which he appeared alongside his son Jesse.

Faber often spoke about his difficult upbringing, part of which he spent living on the streets of Amsterdam as a teenager. In 2008 he set up the Peter Faber Foundation to help young people build confidence, and to “make the switch from destructive to creative energy”. Its motto is “I can do it, I want it, I’m doing it. Now!”

A public memorial service will be held at Het Zonnehuis in Amsterdam-Noord on Monday between 10am and midday.

World.title: Cabinet rules out compensation for drought-hit businesses
World.content:
Despite the country’s continuing water shortage, entrepreneurs feeling the squeeze won’t be receiving any help from the government any time soon.

“There are arrangements in place for the event of a natural disaster, such as the flooding in Limburg in 2021, but we are not there yet,” infrastructure and water management minister Vincent Karremans said while visiting Nijmegen on Thursday.

“We don’t have the money in the account either. We can’t help it that it isn’t raining.”

Maarten Ouboter, a technician for the Amstel, Gooi and Vecht water authority, told DutchNews: “The question is: how much is a government – the public – responsible for the weather? The minister was clear: droughts can happen.”

Low water levels are hurting everyone from inland vessels that can’t sail down dwindling rivers to houseboat owners on the Rhine who have effectively been marooned. Several locks have been closed, ferries have been cancelled and the economically important Twente Canal, reported broadcaster NOS, is also inaccessible.

And while Karremans estimates that the economic damage to businesses runs “into the tens, if not hundreds of millions of euros”, he views the water shortage as an “entrepreneurial risk, after all” – not a natural disaster.

A shortage but not a crisis

For now, the country’s water level remains at 2 – a shortage but not yet a crisis. That could change if the drought continues for another few weeks. But the government maintains its priorities are preserving the country’s dikes and ensuring enough available drinking water, not propping up businesses.

“We are now at a point that the rivers flowing into our low-lying delta have never been so low in August,” said Ouboter, who focuses on the Amsterdam area. “We are comparable to 1947, but that was in November.”

Using a football analogy, he said the drought “in June was ‘second league’; in July it was ‘first league’; in August, it’s Champions League.”

Boosting water storage

Karremans said more water must be stored for the future, including in places like the IJsselmeer and the Volkerak-Zoommeer. The cabinet is currently working on the Freshwater Delta Plan to ensure rainwater captured in the spring, for example, can be used in drier months.

In Amsterdam, an innovative system of wadis – dry water ditches – catches rainwater that can be distributed later where needed and also absorbs extra rainwater to prevent flooding.

“The way we think about water has changed,” said Ton Hilhorst, the chief garden designer at Amsterdam’s Artis zoo. “Water was always seen as the enemy, but now we must keep it in the country, not pump it out.”

Weather forecasters are predicting another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with rain unlikely in the current week.

World.title: Philip Morris rebuked over AI campaign against EU tobacco rules
World.content:
The Dutch advertising standards watchdog RCC has reprimanded tobacco behemoth Philip Morris for an AI-powered ad campaign that it says violated the country’s tobacco advertising ban.

As the EU prepares its biggest tobacco tightening rules in 15 years, the public was invited to share its views via comments.

But a recent investigation by broadcaster NOS and the journalism platform Pointer found that Philip Morris used AI to generate hundreds of fake “citizen” responses opposing tougher EU rules on vapes, which along with other cigarette alternatives like e-cigarettes and heated tobacco, now account for 40% of the company’s revenue.

Here’s how the campaign worked: Philip Morris put up yellow posters carrying QR codes in tobacco shops under the slogan “Your Voice Your Choice.” Scanning the code led to a tool that asked multiple-choice questions and then an option to write a first-person text, which users could then send to the Commission.

The investigation found that some 71% of responses from the Netherlands were written by AI, the second highest after Portugal.

The RCC had several problems with the campaign, including that the text generator was paid for and owned by Philip Morris. The company defended its actions by saying it contributed to the public debate.

“The fact that the statements are framed as a call for public consultation does not detract from their commercial character,” said the watchdog.

The written responses also portray alternative tobacco products positively, which the RCC says constitutes advertising and therefore violates the tobacco advertising ban.

Doctors

In June, a group of doctors and healthcare campaign groups made a formal complaint to the RCC, saying the “misleading” campaign used an AI tool to influence European decision-making on tobacco and nicotine products.

Lawyer Laura van Gijn, who represents the doctors, told NOS that violating the tobacco advertising ban is a criminal offence. “This decision is a clear signal to the tobacco industry that digital influence campaigns do not fall outside the scope of the advertising ban, even when packaged as citizen participation. This precedent is relevant for similar campaigns elsewhere in Europe.”

World.title: No more “shame lips”: Dutch dictionary adds new word for labia
World.content:
Women’s rights groups are applauding the latest addition to the definitive Dutch dictionary Dikke Van Dale of the word labia: vulvalippen, added alongside the word schaamlippen.

While both words mean labia, the old schaamlippen translates as “shame lips”, which the organisations say is stigmatising as compared to the more neutral “vulva lips”.

“We should just mention these parts in our education with children and young people,” artist Esther van der Valk told broadcaster NOS. “People now know that this is a normal word, and with that we can break the taboo.”

Van der Valk is a member of Dolle Mina, the women’s rights group that was founded in the Netherlands in 1969 and has been advocating for the inclusion of vulvalippen in the Dutch dictionary to counter stigmatisation. They’re joined by Schaamteloos, a more recent campaign seeking to change language and attitudes regarding female anatomy.

Body positive

While schaamlippen will remain in the dictionary, the addition of vulvalippen means the word gets official Dutch language status – proof, say the activists, that the normalisation of sexuality via language can be achieved if enough people want it.

Schaamlippen is not the only word where shame is embedded in its name. There’s schaamhaar – “shame hair” – which is the name for pubic hair, schaambeen (shame bone) for pubic bone and even schaamstreek (shame area) for pubic area.

But Schaamteloos says it had to start somewhere, so it picked schaamlippen. “Everyone has pubic hair, a pubic bone, and a pubic area,” says the group, but “only half of us have labia – or ‘shame lips’ … which adds to a disproportionately large amount of trouble due to the taboo on talking about this.”

While some doctors and even the media have taken to using vulvalippen, it’s not yet part of the everyday Dutch vernacular.

That may change when the new anatomically correct word is included in the Dikke van Dale. That’s expected to happen during its next online update, likely this Autumn.

World.title: Four arrested for death threat against Breda mayor
World.content:
Police have arrested four men suspected of threatening to kill Breda mayor Paul Depla, after a photograph found on a football supporter’s phone revealed new evidence for a case that had stalled.

A banner bearing the words “Depla Dood” (Depla dead) was hung on the front of a café in the city’s Meidoornstraat on March 8, when NAC Breda played Feyenoord. Depla reported the threat to the police, but in May prosecutors said the case had halted because the suspects could not be linked to the banner.

A breakthrough came when several NAC supporters were arrested over rioting around the club’s match against Heerenveen on May 10 and their phones were seized, police said. On one of them, officers found a photograph of the banner in which four men could be identified.

The four – three from Breda, aged 16, 32 and 34, and a 24-year-old from Oosterhout – were arrested on Thursday and will be questioned. Threatening a public official carries a maximum prison sentence of four years.

It is unclear what prompted the threat, but broadcaster NOS reported it may have followed a warning from the city council to a different café, which had planned to host a pre-match party for the club’s hardcore supporters.

When the owners called the party off, the group gathered at the Meidoornstraat café instead, where the banner was hung.

Threats and intimidation against Dutch public officials are a growing concern. Some 45% of local and regional political office holders, including mayors, told a 2024 home affairs ministry survey they had faced aggression in the preceding year.

World.title: Warm, dry weekend ahead as drought shows no sign of ending
World.content:
The Netherlands is set for another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with barely a drop of rain likely for the coming week, according to forecasters.

Friday will be calm and dry with temperatures of 21 to 25°, with morning cloud in the north east giving way to sunshine. Saturday will be sunny and slightly warmer, at 25 to 28°, before temperatures climb to around 30° inland on Sunday.

A brief cooler spell will push maximums down to around 25° on Tuesday, but forecasters expect the warmth to return later in the week – without any significant rain.

The dry spell means no let-up for the ongoing drought, which has pushed the Rhine to record low levels and prompted water use restrictions in several regions.

World.title: Childcare benefits falling short for most parents: CBS
World.content:
Almost two-thirds of parents who claim childcare benefits pay more than the government’s maximum hourly rate, leaving them with hundreds of euros in costs the benefit does not cover, according to national statistics agency CBS.

Parents claiming the benefit spent an average of €10,510 on childcare in 2025, of which 68% was covered, up from 65% in 2024. The benefit was raised in both years as a step towards the government plan for near-free childcare.

But childcare providers are free to set their own fees, and the benefit only applies to costs up to a ceiling fixed by the government each year. In 2025, 63% of parents paid more than the maximum rate for at least one child.

On average, parents paid €3,340 towards childcare themselves last year – €2,860 in regular contributions, plus an extra €480 to cover fees above the official maximum.

The share of parents paying over the ceiling varies widely. In Nunspeet, Bloemendaal, Houten and Midden-Delfland, almost 90% pay more than the maximum rate, compared with just 8% on the island of Ameland. The proportion is highest in the provinces of Utrecht and Noord-Holland and lowest in Friesland and Groningen.

Households in the lowest income group paid an average of €1,190 towards childcare, or 11% of the total cost, while the highest earners paid €5,950, just over half the bill.

In total, 719,000 parents claimed the benefit last year for nearly 1.1 million children. More children attended nurseries and after-school clubs, while the number looked after by registered childminders (gastouders) fell by 10,000 to around 95,000.

The cabinet plans to make childcare almost free for working parents from 2029, covering 96% of costs regardless of income – a scheme that has been repeatedly delayed.

World.title: Candidate to lead Polish state history institute rejected in rare clash between houses of parliament
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
