World.title: ‘We couldn’t get over that’: The AFLW norm baffling this Irish import
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Erone Fitzpatrick is a star – All-Australian, Carlton leader and selected in the Irish representative AFLW side – but there’s one thing about Australian rules football that leaves her baffled. Club loyalty – or rather, the lack of it. Hailing from County Laois in Ireland, Fitzpatrick helped lead them to their first Gaelic football title in over 20 years in 2022, before being poached by Carlton for the 2023 season. Carlton’s Erone Fitzpatrick will represent her homeland in the ALFW Aus vs Ireland clash. Joe Armao She played with the same teammates from age four to 23; switching clubs or counties is “unheard of at home”. “Talking to a lot of the Aussies here, they can’t get over how loyal you are to your club and your county throughout your whole career,” Fitzpatrick said. “I would play with the one club for my whole football career, and I would play with the one county for my whole football career, and they couldn’t get over that.



“That’s why we find it really strange, the whole trade period and people leaving clubs and going to different clubs and stuff like that.” Fitzpatrick hopes she can stick with her AFLW side in a similar way. “I would love that,” she said. “You never know what can happen in the future, but I think it would be very weird for me to go anywhere else. I think if you asked a lot of the Irish players, they would say the exact same thing.” Since the AFLW’s inaugural season in 2017, the presence of Gaelic football cross-coders has skyrocketed, with 44 active Irish players in the league and two inactive. Their effect has been profound. The Irish players play a lightning-fast and attacking style. North Melbourne, who have won two consecutive AFLW premierships, currently have five Irish players on their list, while the Brisbane Lions, Adelaide, Geelong and Carlton all have a strong contingent of Irish players. Erone Fitzpatrick is one of 46 Irish players in the AFLW. Joe Armao The impact in Ireland has been seismic as well. On one hand, the game’s popularity has surged, with Irish broadcasters showing AFLW games, dedicated 3am watch parties and growing fan bases on social media.



But the amount of Irish-born players lured to Australia has also left a growing hole in Gaelic football pathways, especially in smaller regions, “I’m from a very small county, not saying that I would have been a big fish, but I probably would have been at home,” Fitzpatrick explains. “For my county to lose like someone like me is hard ... because in a small county, talent is very limited compared to the bigger counties that have a huge pool of talent. “Counties like Mayo have six girls playing in the AFLW – that’s a huge chunk of unbelievable talent from one county.” There’s enough Irish talent in AFLW to make a representative game in the mould of State of Origin possible. Fitzpatrick represented Ireland in that match in Sydney, in front of a sellout crowd. Speaking in the lead-up, Fitzpatrick was thrilled to be part of it. Carlton star Erone Fitzpatrick was a pivotal part of the Blue’s surge into the prelim finals. AFL Photos



“My parents are flying out for the game, which is so important to me, and I’ll also have my aunties, family friends, my grannies’ next door neighbour,” she joked. “I want to make them proud, and I want to make all the young girls proud and know they can chase their dreams and be anything they want in life.” Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 ‘Faceless’ foes to face off as Carlton and St Kilda scrap for wildcard spot Now, the focus is on the upcoming AFLW season, which begins on Sunday at Marvel Stadium when Fitzpatrick’s Blues take on the Saints before the clubs’ men’s teams do the same. The Blues’ women’s side made it to a preliminary final last season, where they fell short against the Lions. It was a meteoric turnaround – Carlton finished 14th in 2024 before introducing a crop of young, extroverted talent in 2025. Fitzpatrick was a pivotal part of the resurgence last year, averaging 17.5 disposals and kicking 13 goals.

World.title: ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret
World.content:
But the true significance of Gaunt’s debut has been shrouded in a family secret for decades, only recently confirmed by DNA testing: Ron Gaunt may well have been Australia’s first Test cricketer of Indigenous heritage.

After moving to Victoria, Gaunt also made his mark in the east, notably as the longtime bowling coach for the Footscray Cricket Club. It was there he set Merv Hughes on the path to a storied career by telling the young all-rounder from Werribee that he was, in fact, a bowler.

“He was quick and used to swing the ball about quite nicely. Especially on the Perth wicket where he used to get a bit of pace and bounce, he was a nasty proposition for a batsman to face. He was certainly a top-rate fast bowler,” Craig told Cricinfo in 2012.

Gaunt’s story was a good one, of a strapping quick bowler with a shock of red hair, who may well have played many more games for Australia had he not been stuck behind the likes of Alan Davidson and Graham McKenzie.

Within a few days, the 23-year-old Gaunt made his debut in Durban, claiming figures of 2-87 in a drawn match under the captaincy of Ian Craig.

In January 1958, a young West Australian fast bowler by the name of Ron Gaunt was flown into South Africa as an injury replacement for the Australian Test team.

Because of its rich wheat farming, York was home to plenty of prosperous families, who shared the land with the Indigenous community.

The municipality of York, about 100 kilometres east of Perth, is WA’s oldest inland town, established in 1831 after being home to the Ballardong Noongar people for thousands of years.

Gaunt’s story also raises a wider question of Australian cricket, and life. How many more gifted athletes of Indigenous heritage have been part of the nation’s story in secret, because of the past strictures of the White Australia policy?

Since then, Ash Gardner, Scott Boland and Brendan Doggett have joined the list of Indigenous Test cricketers. Boland will proudly take the field for Australia in a Test against Bangladesh in Darwin , amidst one of the nation’s largest Indigenous communities, this week.

His debut came a month earlier than the sole women’s Test played by Aunty Faith Thomas at Melbourne’s Junction Oval in February 1958, and decades before Jason Gillespie took the field for Australia in Sydney in 1996.

As the years went by, rumours circulated that the swarthy complexion of some children was down to Spanish ancestry, or even that someone in the family had married a Pacific Island princess. Anything but Indigenous heritage.

The secrecy started around the time of the First World War, when two family members served, including Arthur Gaunt. When he came back from Europe, Arthur listed his mother’s heritage as Maori, the better to receive a gratitude bond of £100 for returned servicemen.

“All this was kept a secret,” says Ron’s nephew, Dudley Gaunt. “There were laws and restrictions, and it just would’ve made their lives difficult. So they hid it away.”

Walter and Matilda raised her eldest son, Arthur, together, but also had other children, including another named Walter. After Walter junior grew up, he married Ruby Morse, and among six children Ron Gaunt was born in York in 1934.

Matilda Gaunt, who was Indigenous, is seated at right. She was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

Matilda was, by all accounts, a formidable figure. Local newspaper reports tell of how, aged 16, she took the local publican to court in York over unpaid wages and won the case. She was a landowner, and after having one child with another man, Matilda married Walter Gaunt, a local bricklayer.

In 1872, John Walkinshaw Cowan, whose brother would marry the revered social reformer and politician Edith Cowan, had a child with an unnamed Aboriginal woman. That child, Matilda Cowan, was Ron Gaunt’s grandmother.

“WA was a very harsh place for Aboriginal people,” says Ron’s niece, Jenny Ewell. “I think they wanted to avoid that, and absolutely because of Ron’s cricket.

It is ironic that two of Gaunt’s three Tests were played against Apartheid South African teams – just another reminder of the complexities facing a young man of mixed race in Australia in the 1950s and ’60s.

Gaunt was among the most promising young fast bowlers in the country, with enough of a competitive streak to indulge in a bit of “Bodyline” bowling for WA in 1956. In a game against Queensland, umpire Colley ordered WA captain Ken Meuleman to change the field, and warned Gaunt about his bowling.

When the Gaunt family moved from York to Perth, as Walter’s building business grew, he purchased land and built a house in a suburb called Rivervale, on the eastern bank of the Swan River. Tellingly, Rivervale was the nearest suburb on the outside of the prohibited area, which was only rescinded in 1954 – well after Ron had started playing club cricket.

In the west, a strict policy was introduced in 1927 to ban the Indigenous community from setting foot into the “Native Prohibited Area” that broadly covered the Perth central business district and select suburbs either side of the Swan River. And in Queensland, an Aboriginal fast bowler named Eddie Gilbert was swift enough to knock the bat out of Don Bradman’s hands, but not to play for Australia.

Much had changed in WA, and Australia, between the late 19th century and the 1930s. Intermarriage between whites and Aboriginal people was first discouraged, then virtually outlawed.

Gaunt, by this time nicknamed “Pappy”, would also mentor Tony Dodemaide, and was instrumental in helping the club win its inaugural first-grade premiership in 1980.

“What he did for me was extraordinary. Without him, I would’ve gone down to Footscray and battled away as a middle-order batsman and part-time bowler. If I had said to Ron, ‘You’re kidding yourself, I’m a batsman’, I’d probably still be plugging away in Footscray thirds now...”

“I reckon I bowled three balls and Ron came down and said you don’t bat any more, you’re a bowler. He stood at the top of my mark for two or three years, just talking bowling, theories, sorting batsmen out, a whole gamut of different things.

“I was a middle-order batsman who bowled maybe second or third change and then got down to Footscray and had a talk to the president, the coach, Ken Eastwood was in on the conversation as seconds captain, and Ron Gaunt was there,” Hughes says.

“Ron absolutely loved playing cricket, he lived and breathed the game, and I think it would have just destroyed him had he not been able to play it. So that’s probably where it came from.”

Hughes remembers Gaunt’s skill as a technical coach, plus his ability to still send down beautiful outswing in the nets. But what sticks with him is the older man’s personal touch – sports psychology before it had the name.

“You could talk to him about anything,” Hughes says. “He could pick up on if you were having a bad day or whatever, and that’s the philosophy I take with kids now. You talk to them, and it’s not just about cricket, but about school, are exams coming up? If guys aren’t concentrating on their bowling, you try to get to the bottom of it, and he used to do that beautifully.

”He knew you had the talent and if you weren’t producing at training he’d try to get to the bottom of it. He’d say, ‘Listen, you’re at training, you can leave that behind, and concentrate on your training’.”

Merv Hughes was mentored by Ron Gaunt at Footscray. Getty

Some earthier incentives came when Hughes and Footscray were fighting for their lives in the 1980 first-grade grand final.

“In the first XI grand final I played in my second year at Footscray, there was 10 and 11 batting, and he just said, ‘Right boys, if you can get to double figures here I’ll buy you a slab’,” Hughes remembers. “How hard do you reckon we worked to get those runs?

“If you did well, he was always there for you. It wasn’t him beating his chest, it was just him patting you on the back and saying, ’Well done’.”

Dodemaide, a couple of years younger than Hughes, can recall watching Gaunt bowl, perhaps planting a seed that led an initially front-on bowler to change his action to allow for the away swingers that netted Dodemaide 10 Test caps.

Australian selector Tony Dodemaide (right). Getty Images

“He had the tracksuit on and was clearly well past playing age, but he went in to bowl a few balls and demonstrate what he was talking about, and he had this beautiful side-on jump and action, and it was just so smooth,” says Dodemaide, now an Australian selector. “I thought, ‘Wow, could I ever bowl like this bloke?’

“Having a couple of Test players around the club was just gold for a young kid like me. He only played a handful of Tests, but that was enough as far as we were concerned – to spend any time around someone who’d played at that level of cricket.”

None of Hughes, Dodemaide or even his fellow Footscray Test cricketer Ken Eastwoood had any idea about Gaunt’s heritage.

“I never knew that, but that’s a real feather in his cap,” Hughes says. “Times have changed for the better. I thought I spent a fair bit of time with him, but it was never mentioned. Back then he might’ve been hiding that heritage.”

There is one former teammate, Lindsay James, who has told Dodemaide that Gaunt did indeed know of his Indigenous heritage, and that the pair discussed it quietly, once, long after both had finished playing and coaching.

“I couldn’t imagine him being a fearsome fast bowler,” Dodemaide says. “He had such a gentle demeanour about him, and very generous with his time and experience.”

After retirement, Gaunt moved to the NSW Central Coast to share more time with his children, Karon and Andrew. Gaunt and their mother had divorced when Andrew was two years old.

“Once a year we used to get to see my father around Christmas time for a month, [and] then he’d have to go back to Victoria to work,” Andrew says. “But when I was around 21-22, I went and stayed with him for a few years, and that was good. He was pretty much just like a mate, he spoke like a mate and that’s how we were.

“I came back to Sydney after a couple of years, and we kept in closer contact, and, eventually, he retired up the Central Coast and I went up and stayed there for a while. But work was back here in Sydney. So I was always going up there weekly, pretty much for years.”

Australian Test players Ron Gaunt (left) who played his first Test against South Africa with captain Bob Simpson and Richie Benaud. "The News" and "The Mail"

Sport in general, and cricket in particular, was never far away from the conversation.

“You had no choice on the TV, it was cricket when it started until it finished, then he’d go, ‘OK it’s yours now’,” Andrew recalls. “He never boasted, he never bragged, that wasn’t him. Other people who knew him would say, ‘That’s Ronnie Gaunt, he used to play for Australia’. But he’d never say that. He wouldn’t talk too much about it – what happens on tour stays on tour almost.”

If Gaunt was taciturn about his cricket achievements, his heritage was buried deeper still, remaining unknown to the family when Ron died in 2012. Eight years later, during COVID-19, Andrew’s half-sister Kellie started digging into family history. Ancestry searches were followed by DNA tests, revealing a hidden Indigenous bloodline.

Indigenous Test star Scott Boland. Getty Images

“One day, out of the blue she gave me a call and said, ‘Andrew, guess what, you’ll never believe it’, and I just said, ‘Nah, get out of here’. And my other sister Karon couldn’t believe it at all.

“Then Kellie got in contact with Jenny, and she took it up and ran with it. It was a such a well-kept secret, and maybe that was a reason why. He may not have played for Australia or got the chances he did if they knew he had Indigenous background.

“I was speaking to my sisters about Jason Gillespie saying, ‘Geez, he’s supposed to be the first person of Indigenous blood to play for Australia’. I started laughing about that and going, ‘Oh man, sorry about that’.”

Ask Andrew what he might have said to his father had he known, and he pauses.

“I’d probably have said, ‘What the hell were you thinking?’” he laughs. “I’m actually quite proud or glad, it just cements that footprint in our family as a full-on Aussie. But I don’t think they looked at it like that.”

While Ron got his mother Ruby’s red hair, Andrew and Jenny are both darker in complexion. Andrew can remember, as a teenager, that Ron got them together at Martin Place in Sydney.

“I met Jenny one time when I was about 16,” he says. “Dad was in Melbourne at the time, but he came up to see us. He wanted me to go and meet my cousin, he goes, ‘Come and meet your cousin’, and Karon said, ‘What about me?’ and he says, ‘Nah, just Andrew’. I thought that was a bit odd.

“That’s the first and last time I met Jenny [who moved to the United States, where she still lives]. But I think Dad was sizing me up with her because we were both darker in complexion. That’s just my take, but my sisters Karon and Kellie thought that made sense.”

After Jenny took up the family research, she passed much of the information onto Dudley Gaunt, who still lives in WA. He has had inconclusive discussions with WA Cricket about Ron’s Indigenous heritage, and has also made attempts to contact the Ballardong Noongar community. Cricket Australia is looking into the Gaunt family story.

“We want to ensure cricket’s heritage fully reflects all those from different backgrounds who have contributed to the game,” a CA spokesman said.

“The stories provided by those exploring family ancestry is an important way to ensure the diverse backgrounds of past players is recognised.”

Dudley says the main issue in his meeting with WA Cricket was not Gaunt’s Aboriginality, “It was whether he accepted his Aboriginality, whether he told people. Did he tell people at South Perth cricket club?

“If he wouldn’t have been able to play cricket, why would he tell anyone at South Perth that he was Aboriginal? It was a different time, they parked it away, hid it and got on with their lives.”

In 2005, the former chief justice of NSW, James Spiegelman, spoke about hidden Aboriginal histories in that year’s Charles Perkins Oration.

“Let me state one undeniable fact: many, probably millions of Australians have an Aboriginal ancestor,” he said. “This should be recognised as an important bond. However, most do not know this fact about their family.

“There was a strong sense of racism involved in the suppression in thousands upon thousands of Australian families of the Aboriginal origins of one or more of their forebears. For most of our history this has been regarded as a matter to be suppressed.

“It appears to me that the process of reconciliation would be advanced by a wider recognition across the broad Australian community that the number of Australians who have Aboriginal ancestors probably amounts to millions.

“The reconciliation process cannot succeed if it is based, contrary to historical fact, solely on maintaining a rigid and categorical distinction between black and white. It will succeed if a significant proportion of those Australians of whom it is true take pride in acknowledging their roots in both communities.”

For Jenny, the secret is itself a significant part of the story.

“I was very proud to find that out myself, to think we’ve got heritage that goes back 60,000 years in Australia,” she says. “But in going back to speak to the family, I found out that the family did know, and didn’t say anything.

“I was shocked, thinking, ‘Gosh they kept it a good secret all those years’. But a lot of it might have been that they wanted to work and get on with their lives. This is my opinion – because Ron was playing cricket and very successful, they wanted that to keep going and that it wasn’t made more difficult for him.”

Andrew recalls one other comment from his father that has taken on new meaning.

“My dad used to tell me, ‘You have a whole other family in the west’,” he says. “It was a big secret, and back then I could understand it. Whereas now I’m like, ‘Wow, that’s cool’.”

World.title: How an Australian mining company was caught in Trump’s tightening Cuba noose
World.content:
Exclusive WorldNorth AmericaForeign relations How an Australian mining company was caught in Trump’s tightening Cuba noose Michael Koziol August 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On the outskirts of a city called Moa, at the south-eastern end of Cuba, flies a Canadian flag. Its maple leaf flaps proudly beside the red triangle and white star of Cuba’s own national banner. The flags mark the Moa Nickel mine, a joint venture between Canadian mining company Sherritt International and Cuban state-owned La Compania General de Niquel. Ore is extracted, shipped to Alberta in Canada and refined into nickel and cobalt. The Canadian flag flies next to the Cuban flag at the Moa Joint Venture, a nickel mine in southeastern Cuba. Google Maps In May, as part of efforts to crush Cuba’s communist regime, the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Moa Nickel. The mine, already hit by fuel shortages after the US choked off Cuba’s Venezuelan lifeline, has shut down – as has Sherritt’s refinery in Fort Saskatchewan, Canada. Now, the Trump administration is doing the same thing to a fledgling gold and copper mine part-owned by an Australian company, Antilles Gold. And in both cases, the solution appears to be the same: sell a stake to the Americans, possibly to friends of US President Donald Trump.



“Their choices are to leave, stay and then have an immense amount of problems, or try to find a saviour,” said John Kavulich, president of the US-Cuba Trade and Economic Council, a New York-based business network. “If I’m an executive of Antilles Gold in Australia, I’m waiting for someone to stick a gun in my stomach. Thus far, that’s the only thing the Trump administration hasn’t done.” ASX-listed Antilles Gold was slapped with US sanctions in early June when its Cuban joint venture, Minera La Victoria, was blacklisted. The company, which is headquartered at an unassuming home in the NSW town of Bowral, owns 50 per cent of the venture through its Cayman Islands-registered subsidiary, Antilles Gold Inc. Its main project is the Nueva Sabana open-pit copper and gold mine in central Cuba, 25 kilometres south-east of Ciego De Avila. According to Antilles’ ASX filings, the earthworks, water supply and site preparation began in early December, and a Chinese company, Xinhua Mining, was given the go-ahead on a $US30 million ($42 million) engineering and construction contract on New Year’s Eve.



Antilles Gold says work has halted while it scrambles to deal with the impact of June’s sanctions. It says the company has submitted a proposal to the US State Department that would involve selling at least 51 per cent of shares in the Caymans-based subsidiary to an acceptable US investor. Who might that be? The company’s chairman, Brian Johnson, won’t say. Neither will Kavulich, who has been working with Antilles Gold. “I can’t go there,” he said. The Moa Nickel mine in Cuba, a joint venture between Canada’s Sherritt International and a state-owned enterprise. Google In the case of Canada’s Sherritt International, its potential saviour is an entity called Gillon Capital – the family office of Heather and Ray Washburne, who happens to be a close ally of Trump. The companies are in exclusive negotiations for Gillon to take a 55 per cent stake in Sherritt at a discount to its closing value on May 15 (it had already crashed from $US0.25 a share to $US0.09 following the US sanctions).



The State Department and US Treasury cleared the way for the talks to take place, but will need to approve any final deal. Washburne is a businessman, investor and real estate developer who co-founded a restaurant chain in Texas. A long-time Republican donor, in 2016 he was described by the Texas Tribune as “Trump’s most visible fundraiser” in Dallas. Ray Washburne, pictured in 2018, was a major fundraiser for Donald Trump in Texas, and was appointed by him to run the Overseas Private Investment Corporation. Getty Images for Concordia Summit In his first term, Trump appointed Washburne to run the Overseas Private Investment Corporation, the federal government’s development bank, and he later served on Trump’s intelligence advisory board. He no longer holds either position. Sherritt’s initial response to the expanded US sanctions was to say it would relinquish its stake in the Cuban venture, which it built over 30 years. But that changed. Bloomberg News reported that Sherritt’s interim chief executive, Peter Hancock, was at home in Canada watching cycling when Washburne called him to make the offer.



“This deal happened because an actor in the United States was able to make a case to the US State Department,” Hancock told Bloomberg. “We were collateral damage in a larger policy objective for the United States.” Washburne doesn’t see it that way at all. Reached by phone on Thursday (US time), he said he was rescuing Sherritt and its mine from certain ruin, and the Trump administration had nothing to do with arranging the deal. US President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on Friday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson “The company was in severe financial straits to begin. I’ve known about the company for years, I’ve followed it, I knew that it had some valuable assets to it,” he told this masthead. “When I saw the sanctions were put in place – I didn’t have any idea they were doing that – I just called the company and said: do you need capital? If I hadn’t come in, it would have already been shut down and gone.”



Gillon Capital was spun out of an existing family office, A. G. Hill Partners, linked to the Hunt family dynasty. Washburne’s wife Heather, née Hill, is a descendant of Texas oil tycoon Haroldson Lafayette Hunt Jr, who secured the rights over much of the enormous East Texas Oil Field. Related Article Explainer

Trump diplomacy ‘Cuba is finished’: What does Trump want with the island nation? Gillon does not own any other mining interests at present, although the family – through oil heirs Nelson and William Hunt – once owned part of one of the world’s largest silver mines, in Idaho. Washburne says he cold-called Sherritt himself when he saw the Canadian miner was in trouble. “I literally just found the guy’s phone number … It had nothing to do at all with the administration. I had no discussion with them at all.” He said he was not aware of Australian company Antilles Gold and its Cuba venture, and was not in discussions with them. But he was interested, and asked for their contact details. Washburne’s late mother was Australian, born in Sydney between the wars.



Antilles Gold chairman Johnson told this masthead that the company had identified a suitable American investor, and it was not Gillon Capital, although he would not disclose who it was. The firm’s proposal to the State Department remained confidential, he said. The Australian government confirmed it had engaged with Antilles Gold and US officials on the matter, but would not answer questions about those discussions. The State Department did not respond to inquiries. Cuba’s former president Raul Castro, 94, arrives at a gathering for International Workers’ Day in Havana on May 1, 2026. AP John Kirk, a professor emeritus of Latin American studies at Dalhousie University in Nova Scotia, Canada, said it was noteworthy that the State Department appeared to have no objection to Gillon Capital taking over the mine in Cuba. “Clearly, Trump is supporting his friends in the stealthy takeover of Cuban commerce,” Kirk said. “I suspect that a similar path will be found for Antilles Gold. In both cases, greed, hypocrisy and bullying have been implemented by the Trump administration.”



ASIC records show Antilles Gold was first registered in South Australia in 1984 as Aytox Pty Ltd. It has been through several name changes; as EnviroGold and Panterra Gold, it developed a mine in the Dominican Republic in the 2010s. The company had been turning its attention to a second Cuban project, a planned gold, silver and antimony mine on the Isla de la Juventud (the Isle of Youth). Infill drilling was supposed to start at the La Demajagua mining concession in the second half of this year, until the sanctions hit. A man pulls a cart carrying drinking water during a power outage in Havana, Cuba, last week. AP Photo/Ramon Espinosa For foreign firms, the main effect of US sanctions is on banking. Any company using US dollars is likely to be cut off by a financial institution. Even if there’s doubt, banks are generally risk-averse and won’t want to take the chance, Kavulich says. The US continues to impose new sanctions on Cuba and its interests. On Thursday, it designated a number of entities and people related to the procurement and sustainment of Cuban weapons.



“They went after the Cuban companies and ministries that everyone knows about first,” Kavulich says. “Now, they’re going granular, and they’re going deeper and deeper and deeper.” Related Article Updated

Cuba US brings criminal charges against former Cuban president Raul Castro Asked whether he thought the Trump administration’s approach to foreign companies operating in Cuba was effectively a shakedown, he said: “One person’s shakedown is another person’s benevolent opportunity to do what’s right.” Last month, the State Department released a 100-page report on the dangers Cuban communism posed to America and the Western world. Havana was “a staging ground where the ambitions of Moscow, Beijing, and Tehran converge with the radical movements operating inside our own borders”, it concluded, referring to the far-left. The report frames Cuba as a major security threat, thereby laying the groundwork for potential military intervention, which has been the subject of much speculation over the past six months. Meanwhile, it keeps tightening the noose on the country’s collapsed economy.



“They certainly can’t wait us out,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told US news site Axios. “Every time they create a new mechanism in which they try to get out of the noose, we just close it off.” Emily Morris, an economist and researcher specialising in Cuba at University College London, said the administration’s endgame was not clear, but “if any deal were done, it could well be a deal that allows US businesses in [to Cuba] but not others”. Paolo Spadoni, an associate professor at Augusta University and a recognised Cuba expert, said the primary motivation of Trump’s intervention was political, rather than a play for resources. “I think what he wants is to achieve what other presidents for many decades have not been able to achieve,” he said. “And there are economic benefits down the road.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘It’s not easy. It’s not glamorous’: How Matt Preston found a renewed sense of purpose on TV
World.content:
CultureTV & radioAustralian TV ‘It’s not easy. It’s not glamorous’: How Matt Preston found a renewed sense of purpose on TV Bridget McManus August 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thigh-deep in the freezing shallows off South Australia’s Fleurieu Peninsula, Matt Preston is gathering pipis at dawn with Ngarrindjeri fishermen for his new series, Matt Preston’s Plating Locally. In the grey early hours of the morning he will cook the shellfish with pasta on the beach, signature cravat snug against the wind, with a skeleton film crew capturing the simple recipe. Former MasterChef Australia judge Matt Preston is engaging with local growers for his new series, Matt Preston’s Plating Locally. Such working conditions are a far cry from the lavish kitchen set where he made his name, and the shiny floor studios where he dipped his toe in light entertainment (three years on he still salsas with his Dancing with the Stars partner Jessica Raffa, while The Masked Singer gifted him a thing for karaoke). But since appearing in March on SBS’ The Hospital: In the Deep End, this original MasterChef Australia judge is seeking profound connections. Of course, the work of frontline medical staff that so affected him is very different to that of food producers, but Preston is determined to “choose stuff that will challenge people … it’s all passion projects from now on”. “Plating Locally has a purpose, in that these stories need to be told,” he says. “Whether you’re spending an hour in chilly, shark-infested waters off Kangaroo Island on your oyster lease, or raking pipis, or diving for abalone, or getting up at five to tend your flock – it’s not easy. It’s not glamorous. And it doesn’t necessarily pay that well.”



Related Article Australian TV Meet the architect who designs the houses on The Block On Kangaroo Island he meets oyster farmers affected by the South Australian algal bloom. “When they couldn’t work, they couldn’t sell,” he says. “There was that sense of them feeling abandoned, forgotten and unsupported.” Across six episodes Preston visits producers and growers from Margaret River and the Barossa Valley to the Limestone Coast, the Tamar and Yarra valleys, and Marlborough in New Zealand. Along with indulging his senses at wineries, a garlic farm, an artisan buttery and a cheese festival, he fly-fishes for trout and dives into a hidden farm sinkhole. “I’m not Bear Grylls,” he says, laughing. “You’ve got to be mindful that you’re not in your natural environment.” Following to the source the produce he has written about for his newspaper columns for decades proves a great joy, and an eye-opener. “Oh my gosh, the hazelnuts that came out of the Tamar Valley were big and juicy! And to go and look at the king salmon farms in [New Zealand’s] Milford Sound and work out why they don’t have the same negative connotations as we have with salmon farming, that was fascinating. That product is unbelievable. We did it raw, and just the belly flap on the barbecue. It was delicious.”



Matt Preston in WA’s Margaret River for his new series Plating Locally. Preston is adamant every morsel featured on the series really is as good as he says it is. “We picked up some King George whiting [from a market] to shoot in King Island,” he recalls. “It didn’t look stunning. At the place we were staying the son said, ‘I’ll go and catch you some’. He caught us three whiting. When it’s that fresh, it’s magical.” Related Article ★★★★

Review Australia, I’m begging you: give this bonkers show a chance Drawing the best out of those who are camera-shy is a skill Preston honed on his 11 seasons as a judge on MasterChef Australia. “Put them in an environment where they’re comfortable and then they’ll tell you stuff. The story can be massive or it can be really small, but equally powerful and touching.” There was one precious moment that was not captured on camera. “We flew out to one of the islands and the pilot’s mum baked scones for us. Having a cup of tea and a warm scone on an island, those are the moments when you pinch yourself,” he says.

World.title: The freedom to enjoy a Sunday morning, and a timely reminder of what made it possible
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsReligion Opinion The freedom to enjoy a Sunday morning, and a timely reminder of what made it possible Melissa Coburn Contributor August 9, 2026 — 5:30am

August 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On a sparkling Sunday morning, along a coastal track, runners and walkers are out in force. A few fathers jog along, pushing prams to the tune of bright, tinkling nursery rhymes, perhaps giving sleep-deprived partners some extra time in bed. On a Sunday morning walk, enjoying freedom’s privileges, one is reminded it is all thanks to the Anzacs, such as these at Anzac Cove, Gallipoli, during World War I. State Library of NSW A fit, grey-haired woman wearing gloves extracts rubbish from the straggly scrub on the edge of the beach. She is barefoot. Her pink sandals sit on the low stone wall above the beach, like dogs waiting outside the supermarket, conspicuous and incomplete without their owner. Further along, swimmers, in heavy-duty wetsuits, emerge from the sea, perhaps training for a dive in deeper waters. The salty sea air, fresh and cleansing, drifts over to me, full of the promise of holidays to come and dips and books to devour to the soothing whispering of the waves.



Over at a beachside cafe, a kingly infant is frowning, the unwilling participant in his parents’ attempt to re-enter the adult world of cafes and sedentary seaside coffee drinking. There are dogs meeting dogs with the same exuberance of a child encountering another child with a ball. One dog, carrying a Frisbee in his mouth, excites a passing Labrador, who tenses playfully, ready to go fetch. There’s a playground pirate ship, its middle missing as if blown out by a cannon. A parent holds a toddler high in the air near the ship’s upper deck for a bird’s-eye view, while older children, thin and swift, rush in and out of the ship’s compartments, playing hide and seek. Adults walk past the ship without a backward glance; it has no currency for them. Star-shaped purple wild flowers grow in the bushland, and long grasses cast shadows on the beach track as the currawong calls contentedly overhead. To be among all of this is to be free.



Nestled in the grass by the path is a flat plaque. It records that on February 25, 1915, Alexander Henry White, born in Ballarat, left for the First World War. He died less than six months later, on August 7, 1915, while leading his men of the 8th Light Horse Regiment in the first line of the ill-fated charge at the Battle of the Nek, Gallipoli. The plaque honours his memory. A crocheted poppy rests in the dirt beneath the plaque, faded and bleached by the sun. Like Poe’s tell-tale heart, it draws my attention, seeming to implore those who pass by not to forget the soldiers whose sacrifice has made our freedom possible. We must not forget. We must remember those who fought for our peace, who showed courage, especially when victory was unlikely. Their selfless acts rise above the mists of time, beyond a hundred years and more, and blare like trumpets in my ears as I walk in the sunshine, free as a bird, on a normal Sunday morning. Thanks to them. Melissa Coburn is a Melbourne writer.

World.title: House price corrections come and go, let’s not overreact this time
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney house prices House price corrections come and go, let’s not overreact this time The Herald's View August 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s twin urban giants – Sydney and Melbourne – are leading a broad-based downturn in house prices. Nationally, dwelling values have fallen by 2 per cent since their peak in March, according to data published last week by property information firm Cotality. In both Sydney and Melbourne the decline has been a little over 5 per cent. Rising interest rates triggered the slump. The Reserve Bank of Australia’s three rate hikes between February and May lifted its benchmark cash rate to 4.35 per cent, the equal highest level in 15 years. The Sydney property market is experiencing a correction, but it’s not unusual. Peter Rae Federal government reforms that will introduce a less-generous method for calculating capital gains tax and curbs to negative gearing from July next year have also affected investor demand for property.



The price slump has prompted some breathless predictions of property market doom. But corrections have always been a feature of the housing market. Indeed, in our story by Shane Wright today, Westpac chief economist Luci Ellis predicts that the current “airpocket” will likely dissipate by next year. Related Article Property prices End of the super-cycle: Big call on the national property market Domain price data shows that Sydney’s median house prices fell by 14 per cent between June 2017 and March 2019 after authorities introduced targeted lending restrictions to curb risky borrowing. Prices took off again in mid-2020 when interest rates were slashed to “emergency” levels near zero amid the economic disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic (Sydney’s median house price rose by about 35 per cent between June 2020 and June 2022). There was another downturn in 2022 when the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates sharply in a bid to combat the inflationary surge that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine; house prices in Sydney fell by about 8 per cent that year. The latest decline in home values should also be weighed against longer-term price trends – Domain’s latest figures show Sydney’s median house price is 66 per cent higher than a decade ago, despite the recent market weakness.



There is broad agreement that high house prices have locked many young people out of the property market, especially in Sydney. Related Article Property prices Big four banks expect property market to feel pain through 2027 Recent polling for this masthead by the Resolve Political Monitor found 61 per cent of respondents supported a decline in home values. A majority across every age, political and income group agreed that prices were too high. Federal government changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing aim to assist first home buyers to get a foothold in the market. So far, households are coping well with higher interest rates and lower house prices. In a speech last month, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said that the number of home borrowers experiencing negative equity (when a property is worth less than the mortgage secured against it) “remains very limited”. Some economists warn that further house price declines could undermine consumer confidence and dampen household spending.



But there is no evidence of that happening so far – figures made public by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Tuesday showed discretionary spending by households rose by a robust 6.7 per cent in the year to June, the fastest pace of annual growth since mid-2023. Even if the housing downturn starts to take a toll on the broader economy, the RBA’s recent steps to tighten monetary policy mean it has plenty of scope to cut interest rates to support activity. Jordan Baker sends an exclusive newsletter to subscribers each week. Sign up to receive her Note from the Editor.

World.title: Three months after Frawley’s death, Loewe suffered another personal heartbreak
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Three months after Frawley’s death, Loewe suffered another personal heartbreak Danny Russell August 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Stewart Loewe remembers the late Danny Frawley in different ways at different times. When Loewe sets foot on a golf course, he thinks of his old teammate, the larrikin – the version of Frawley that “never lost a ball”, despite spraying them all over the course. St Kilda teammates and friends Stewart Loewe (left) and Danny Frawley after beating Fitzroy by one point at Moorabbin in 1990. The Age He would be the first to emerge from the bushes, having always found “his” ball. When Loewe heads north for a holiday, he remembers Frawley the practical joker.



It reminds him of the times he spent with Frawley, the late Trevor Barker and their partners on Hamilton Island on a yacht owned by Anita Frawley’s parents. Loewe would leave a fishing line in the water overnight, not knowing that his teammates had anchored his hook with a sneaker when he went to bed. “I’d wake up in the morning, and I can hear them giggling now, and I’d go, ‘I’ve got one, I’ve got one’, and I’m just dragging up a dead weight, which is my shoe,” he says. Loewe (right), Garry Lyon, Tony Lockett delivered a stirring pre-match address at the inaugural Spud’s Game in 2021. AFL Photos But as the AFL enters the sixth edition of Spud’s Game at Marvel Stadium on Sunday night, a clash between St Kilda and Carlton to support the mental health message, Loewe remembers the shade as much as the light.



“There was a very complex person behind, you know, the Bounce [on Fox Footy], and you know his persona on Triple M,” Loewe says. “There was a proud father and a proud spud farmer, and someone who was trying to make a mark in corporate AFL and coaching, and he was wrestling all those demons and wrongly thinking that he failed in a lot of them, as we all do when we don’t win a flag, or you’re not a successful premiership coach.” Frawley, the 240-game veteran and much-loved former captain of the Saints, took his own life in 2019. He was 56. It is why it is important, Loewe says, to treat Spud’s Game as a reminder that it is OK to talk to people about your own vulnerabilities. “My life hasn’t been rosy,” Loewe says. “I lost a sister to suicide three months after Danny [in December 2019].



Saints player Dan Butler and assistant coach, and former teammate of Frawley, Robert Harvey at the Danny Frawley Centre in Moorabbin. Penny Stephens “I had a [family member] who was diagnosed bipolar, and I’d lived my whole childhood kind of burying it deep down inside and not really talking about it and being totally embarrassed by it. “But, you know, I think it is liberating to see what Danny did [in discussing mental health]. He was so brave to come out and try and talk about it, and take it all on headfirst and front on. “Some days are pretty shit, and you know we can express that and deal with it the right way, healthily, and move on to the next day.” Loewe said his sister Elizabeth had tried to take her own life 22 years earlier on the eve of the 1997 grand final – St Kilda lost to Adelaide by 31 points after leading by 13 points at half-time. Loewe and Nathan Burke were co-captains.



“I have not talked about it apart from privately to a few people, and I just buried it,” Loewe says. “I buried it in ’97, and didn’t even contemplate talking about it until probably, you know, after Danny’s death, and it affected me greatly. “The way I dealt with it was, you know, taking it from a, ‘You’re selfish’ and the wrong angle and not really having any empathy and understanding and appreciation … which is probably very common, rather than just listening and understanding. “I loved my sister, and I’ve only got one sibling, and it was tragic, but you know, it’s taught myself and my mother and my father, and our immediate family, a lot about ourselves.” Loewe says he is happy to talk about his sister now in the “context of what we’re doing this week … because, you know, I’m quite a private person and haven’t really wanted to talk about it [publicly], having already talked about it with the right people”.



Loewe’ story has been entwined with Frawley since his former captain’s death. He spoke at St Kilda’s best-and-fairest night two days after Frawley died, spoke at his great mate’s funeral the following week, and remains “very tight” with Anita Frawley and her and Danny’s daughters – Chelsea, Danielle and Keeley. Anita Frawley has spoken during a public hearing for the inquiry into concussion and repeated head trauma in contact sports. AAP Loewe has often addressed the St Kilda playing group, but will have only one official duty on Sunday. He will take part in The Hardest Kick charity challenge alongside Brendan Fevola, weather guru Jane Bunn and social media personality DJ Checkers on Marvel Stadium between the Sunday double-header – St Kilda and Carlton’s AFLW sides trade blows from 4.35pm, while the men’s team will fight for a finals berth from 7.20pm.



“Then I’ll go into the function with Anita [Frawley] and the kids, and celebrate a great day with a few friends and family, and reminisce a little bit, and hopefully watch the Saints get a victory,” he said. Loewe says he remains happy to help promote Spud’s Game – which raises money for the Danny Frawley Centre and Black Dog Institute – because it helps promote discussion about mental health. Editor's pick Explainer

Concussion crisis What are CTE and concussion and how do they affect athletes? “That’s probably the biggest learning for myself over the big journey – that it’s not not tough to share a vulnerability with somebody who’s close and can help and can be an ear, and hopefully prevent you from going down the path that eventually that Danny did,” he said. “I’m proud to say that I’ve done a fair bit of work over the last couple of years, and I think it helped me and put me in a really good spot, and not say that my life was ever bad, but I feel like ... I’m viewing life through a different lens – a lot more appreciative, a lot more, I suppose, respectful of what other people are going through, and you know, just understanding the importance of gratitude and living life.”



Coroner Paresa Spanos found in February 2021 that Frawley had low-stage chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) – a form of brain disease linked to repeated blows to the head – and was a potential contributor to the depression that Frawley suffered in the years preceding his death. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14, or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636.

World.title: Warnings issued as heavy rain heads to Bay of Plenty, Northland
World.content:
MetService is forecasting heavy rain for Northland and eastern Bay of Plenty as a front moves eastward across northern and central North Island on Sunday and early Monday.

An orange rain warning is in place for the ranges of eastern Bay of Plenty. MetService forecasts 70 to 90mm of rain, peaking at 10 to 20mm/h expected. The warning is for 12 hours from 3pm Sunday to 3am Monday.

It warned that streams and rivers may rise rapidly, and that surface flooding, slips and difficult driving conditions were possible. Avoid low-lying areas and drive cautiously, it said.

There was minimal chance of the warning being upgraded to red.

A yellow rain watch is in place for the north and east of Northland. MetService forecasts periods of heavy rain that may approach warning levels.

There was a low risk of localised downpours that could briefly boost rainfall rates to 25 to 40mm/h, it said, and a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning. The watch is until 8pm Sunday.

World.title: Mistake to omit creative arts technologies from new school subjects, drama teachers say
World.content:
*This story has been updated to clarify comments made by Annette Thomson.

The drama teachers' association says the government has made a mistake by omitting technologies that support the creative arts from its list of new industry-led school subjects.

The nine subjects would be developed by industry skills boards to provide clear pathways to further training and jobs for secondary school students in Years 12-13.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama New Zealand said it should have included a subject that covered areas like lighting, sound, staging, costume, and set design.

The organisation's president Annette Thomson said failing to do so would sever students' pathway into industries such as film and television that had critical skill shortages.

Whakaari Aotearoa Drama president Annette Thomson. Supplied / Whakaari Aotearoa Drama NZ

She said currently teens could earn credits toward an NCEA qualification in areas like lighting or sound, but that would not be possible under the new qualification being introduced in 2029 because students would have to study entire subjects and there was no subject that covered those skills.

Thomson said the decision endangered the government's plan to grow the creative sector's economic contribution to $22 billion a year by 2030.

"We feel like they're not really thinking about some of these things that are actually important. They do actively contribute to GDP and to our students," she said.

"All we're seeing is a cutting, a reducing, a narrowing of subjects in the arts."

World.title: National promises Budget Responsibility Rules if elected
World.content:
The National Party will commit to three so-called Budget Responsibility Rules aimed at returning to surplus, cutting debt and keeping taxes low, if elected.

Leader Christopher Luxon and finance spokesperson Nicola Willis made the announcement at Parliament on Sunday.

The Budget Responsibility Rules

Prioritising a return to surplus in 2028/29 and staying in surplus over time so the country's debt curve bends down

Getting debt down below 40 per cent of GDP and keeping it there over time

Keeping taxes low by cutting Crown expenditure as a share of the economy down towards 30 percent of GDP

Willis said the rules reflected a more "volatile world" where borrowing costs had risen and international rating agencies were watching New Zealand closely.

"As a small, commodity-exporting country a long way from anywhere, without a deep pool of domestic savings to fall back on, New Zealand carries more risk than bigger countries when the next earthquake, pandemic or global shock hits.

"That is why these rules are so important for any government. The only way to be ready for the next crisis is to get our books in order now, while conditions allow it," Willis said.

Nicola Willis speaking to media. RNZ/Lauren Crimp

Budget 2026 forecasted a return to a budget surplus in 2028/29 from a mix of an increased tax take, controls on government spending, capital projects and a reduction in borrowing and debt service costs.

The announcement follows a rough week for Luxon, who began it apologising for comments about businesses in Rotorua.

He's also been criticised for his inability to discipline coalition partner Winston Peters and his off-the-cuff call for a referendum on MMP which caught his caucus off guard.

However he won some reprieve on Friday, with the latest Taxpayers' Union Curia poll putting National on 31 percent and predicting the coalition's return to power, along with a steep drop in support for the existing opposition parties.

National released its full election candidate list on Saturday afternoon, largely preserving the existing hierarchy.

World.title: 80% of road travel out of Wellington wouldn't be possible after 7.5 magnitude quake - study
World.content:
A study simulating what would happen to Wellington's road network in a major earthquake has found some parts would be cut off for months.

The simulation assessed the disruption that would be caused by a 7.5 magnitude quake on the Wellington Fault.

The researchers referenced a 2011 study that estimated a 10 percent chance such an earthquake would strike in the next 100 years.

They simulated traffic using parameters like driver reaction time and jam density then applied it to a map of the North Island based on a previous study assessing the infrastructure damage caused by such an earthquake.

On the map, several key roads had been closed including multiple stretches of State Highway 1, Hutt Road, Grant Road, Curtis Street and Chaytor Street.

In the immediate three-day aftermath, the researchers found 68 percent of trips into the Wellington region and 82 percent of trips out of Wellington would be infeasible.

After three months, that reduced to 25 percent of trips into Wellington and 49 percent of trips out of Wellington.

They found Lower Hutt, followed by Wellington City, would be most impacted.

Researchers also found successful trips were much slower, with simulated traffic spreading onto urban detour routes which increased travel times.

But the researchers acknowledged the simulation was limited by assuming demand for travel would remain steady, while in reality many motorists would baulk at the travel time and decide not to drive.

"While this assumption enabled stress-testing of network performance under disruption, it may overestimate congestion and trip cancellations by not accounting for behavioural adaptation during recovery," the paper said.

The researchers said the results highlighted the importance of spending on critical roads to ensure they stayed resilient.

World.title: Person in critical condition after stabbing in Central Auckland
World.content:
One person is in hospital with serious injuries after an alleged stabbing in Central Auckland overnight.

Emergency services were called to Karangahape Road near Pitt Street at 4:20am.

A Hato Hone St John spokesperson said ambulance crews assessed and treated one patient who was transported to Auckland City hospital in a critical condition.

Detective senior sergeant Greg Brand said two people had been taken into custody.

A prisoner from the Mt Eden Corrections Facility was taken to hospital on Saturday evening.

World.title: Hamilton armed robbers found sleeping on mattress in garage after targeting Four Square for vapes
World.content:
As three people armed with weapons and wearing hoods ran into a Four Square supermarket, jumping the front counter, a staff member wondered what the noise was.

Coming out of the kitchen, she walked towards the till and was confronted by Jayden Bint, 24, and his two co-offenders, holding either tyre irons or hedge clippers.

One of them approached her and hit the door to the kitchen with a tyre iron, scaring her and causing her to lock herself inside the kitchen.

Bint's co-offender, meanwhile, stripped the cupboards of vape products and cigarette lighters and handed them to him.

Bint recently appeared in the Hamilton District Court for sentencing on charges of aggravated robbery, motor vehicle conversion, theft of a motor vehicle, breaching release conditions, and two charges of failing to attend court.

Court documents state that two cars were stolen from around Hamilton for the robbery - one from York St, the other from Silverdale Rd - during Waitangi weekend this year.

At 7.27am on 6 February, Bint and two others arrived at the Four Square in Cambridge in a white Toyota Aqua.

Two staff members were working; one was stacking shelves and the other was in the kitchen near the till.

The trio, all wearing disguises, ran in, with Bint's associates jumping over the counter.

After the staff member locked herself in the kitchen, the associates emptied the cigarette cupboard and passed the stolen items to Bint.

All three fled the store and drove to Epping Place in Hamilton, where they dumped the car.

They then jumped into the second car before dumping it in Rachel Place.

Police then received information that the trio had been seen entering a property in Duke St, Hamilton.

There, the defendants were found asleep on a mattress in a garage, two of them still wearing clothing matching that seen during the robbery.

A Nike backpack also contained some of the stolen lighters and vapes.

Addiction 'plainly entrenched'

Bint had earlier accepted a sentence indication from Judge Philip Crayton, who adopted an overall starting point of four years and seven months before applying discounts for Bint's guilty plea and youth.

The judge then took into account Bint's criminal history, which included violence and firearm offending.

He also noted Bint's drug addiction, which he said was "plainly entrenched" in that history.

"It is going to be important that you take steps to try and address that [addiction], otherwise you are just going to be back before the court getting longer and longer sentences."

Judge Crayton issued Bint a first strike under the Three Strikes legislation, and a firearms prohibition order, "due to the risk you pose to public safety".

He jailed Bint for two years and 11 months.

The co-offenders are being dealt with in the Youth Court on the matter.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Privacy experts warn of gaps in NZ law, as camera glasses hit Kmart shelves
World.content:
Privacy experts are warning that wearable camera technology, dubbed by some as "pervert glasses", expose significant gaps in New Zealand's laws.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills said the devices, which were often marketed as smart glasses, were "essentially a computer on your face", combining cameras, microphones, speakers and AI-powered functions in everyday wearable technology.

The Anko Camera Glasses. Supplied / Kmart

Her warning comes as Kmart begins selling its Anko Camera Glasses for just $99, a price point expected to make the technology far more accessible than premium smart glasses such as Meta's Ray-Ban range.

She said that while the glasses offered some benefits, especially as assistive technology for people with disabilities, the technology's growing popularity raised serious privacy concerns.

"We expect to be recorded in some places, such as by CCTV cameras in supermarkets," Mills said.

"But we certainly don't expect to have that everywhere we go."

Mills said that unlike smartphones, which required users to visibly raise a device before taking a photo or recording video, smart glasses could capture footage far more discreetly, making it difficult for bystanders to know whether they were being filmed.

She said overseas cases had already shown how wearable cameras could be misused, including secret recordings in bathrooms and people approaching women in public before uploading the footage to social media without their consent.

Mills said future developments, including facial recognition technology, could make the privacy implications even more significant.

"You could literally look at someone and say, 'Tell me everything there is about this person'. That can make someone feel very vulnerable."

Laws designed for organisations, not individuals

Mills believed New Zealand's privacy framework had a fundamental weakness when it came to wearable technology.

"Our privacy regulations are primarily aimed at protecting individuals, but they are targeted at organisations and what organisations do," she said.

"They are not set up to deal with personal information collected by individuals."

While existing laws could apply to intimate recordings, harmful digital communications and some forms of stalking, Mills said many everyday uses of camera glasses may fall outside current legal protections.

Her concern extended beyond what people record.

Once footage was uploaded to cloud services, it could be processed, analysed and potentially shared in ways many users - and the people they record may not fully understand.

"I think we need to come up with not just regulations that deal with the use, but also controls that deal with the deployment of these devices," she said.

University of Canterbury professor Annette Mills. Supplied / University of Canterbury

Minister of Justice Paul Goldsmith said the government may consider "taking advice on the matter" in the next parliamentary term.

'Serious privacy harms'

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner said the Privacy Act was largely focused on regulating the actions of businesses and organisations, not individuals and it applied regardless of what technology was used.

"Tools like CCTV, drones, and smart glasses make it easier for individuals to record each other. If individuals do not use them in a responsible manner, that can lead to serious privacy harms," a spokesperson said.

It said that individuals using glasses to film covertly should be aware that their actions might breach the Privacy Act if the collection, use or disclosure of the personal information was highly offensive to a reasonable person.

"Other laws are also likely to be relevant, such as the Harmful Digital Communications Act, stalking offences or other crimes under the Crimes Act."

Surveillance concerns extend beyond the wearer

Meanwhile, University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara raised questions about the companies behind the devices.

University of Auckland commercial law professor Gehan Gunasekara. RNZ / Phil Pennington

His concern was not simply that individuals may misuse camera glasses, but that platforms operating the technology could collect vast amounts of information about where people went, what they looked at and how communities behaved.

"The platform also knows all of that information," he said.

"They can map trends, see where people travel and the kinds of stores they shop at."

Even where companies anonymised data before using it to improve artificial intelligence systems, Gunasekara said the aggregated information remained commercially valuable and raised broader questions about privacy and data sovereignty.

A 'game-changing' technology for blind New Zealanders

However, not everyone saw the technology as a threat.

Blind Low Vision New Zealand chief executive Andrea Midgen described AI-enabled smart glasses as the most significant technological advancement her community had seen.

Blind Low Vision chief executive Andrea Midgen. Supplied / Blind Low Vision NZ

The glasses could read street signs, restaurant menus and other visual information aloud while allowing users to keep both hands free for a white cane or guide dog.

"This is the most exciting game changer thing that we've had in technology for our community ever," Midgen said.

She acknowledged privacy concerns but said they stemmed from how people chose to use technology, rather than the technology itself.

"This is just a different form of what already happens with smartphones," she said.

'Use responsibly' - Kmart

A Kmart Group spokesperson confirmed that its Anko Camera Glasses were available to buy in New Zealand.

"The Anko Camera Glasses are part of an established and increasingly mainstream category of wearable technology, with similar products available globally from major technology and eyewear brands. Like other products in this category, they allow users to capture photos and video while also providing audio and connectivity features," the spokesperson said.

"As with any device capable of recording images, we expect customers to use the product responsibly, respectfully and in accordance with applicable laws and community expectations around privacy."

The Ministry of Justice said there were no current plans to introduce a regulatory response specific to the issue of smart glasses.

World.title: Fijian rugby pro, 26, dies of suspected heat stroke after training
World.content:
Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi has died of suspected heat stroke after a training session in Japan. He was 26.

His death was announced on Saturday by his team, Kyushu Electric Power Kyuden Voltex — known as Kyushu KV.

The Japanese second-division club said Vunilagi died on Friday after falling ill on Monday and being hospitalised.

"After team practice on Monday … Saimoni displayed symptoms consistent with severe heat stroke," the team said in a statement Saturday.

"He was transported to a medical facility for treatment, but despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away."

Kyushu KV is based in Fukuoka, a city in southwestern Japan. Temperatures there reportedly reached around 35C on Monday.

"The players, staff, and all team associates are devastated by this sudden news," the team said.

Back rower Vunilagi joined Kyushu KV last month, having previously played in the Japanese top flight with Tokyo Sungoliath.

"Although Saimoni had only recently joined Kyushu KV, his generous spirit and powerful style of play had raised high hopes for his contributions in the upcoming season," Kyushu KV added.

"We humbly pray for the repose of his soul and extend our heartfelt condolences to his bereaved family."

The club supplied no other details surrounding the death.
